Jackson County assessment and collection offices

Two county departments split the work. Assessment values every parcel, and the Department of Collection mails bills and takes payment. For what the house is worth on paper, call Assessment at 816-881-1330. For what you owe or how to pay, call Collection at 816-881-3232.

Assessment keeps real property customer service at 1300 Washington St. in Kansas City and individual personal property at the Historic Truman Courthouse, 112 W. Lexington in Independence. Both counters open at 8 a.m. and close at 5 p.m. on weekdays and are closed on county holidays. Collection also works from both courthouses and takes email at Collections@jacksongov.org.

Before listing, pull your parcel record from the county's public property access portal. It shows the assessed figures that the bill is built from.

Jackson County at a glance

Jackson County is on the Kansas border in western Missouri, with two county seats, Independence and Kansas City. It has 19 communities, among them Blue Springs, Grandview, Lee's Summit, Raytown, Oak Grove, Grain Valley and Sugar Creek. They all share one assessment and collection system, and each taxing district adds its own levy line to the statement.

The 2025 estimate is 732,994 residents in 344,038 housing units. Owners live in 59.1 percent of homes, and the median owned home is valued at $230,500. Median household income is $68,577 and typical gross rent is $1,197. Owners with a mortgage report a median of $1,639 a month in owner costs, taxes included.

Due date and how to pay

The bill is due December 31. The county mails bills during November, and the 2025 mailing was expected to finish by December 12. If nothing has arrived by about December 8, call the Collector, because an unreceived bill carries the same deadline.

A mailed check counts only if USPS stamps it by year end, and the county suggests mailing several days ahead because drop-box mail does not always get a same-day postmark. Make checks payable to the Jackson County Collector with the property account number on them. Online payment at payments.jacksongov.org ends at 11:40 p.m. on December 31, and the two courthouse drop boxes lock at midnight that night. Cash never goes in a drop box.

Paying online costs a $2.00 transaction charge, plus $1.25 for an e-check or 2.75% for a debit or credit card. Paying in person or by check avoids those add-ons.

How to contest an assessment

Start with the Board of Equalization, an independent panel of county taxpayers that now sits only at 1300 Washington in Kansas City. Watch the Board's page for the next application window.

Evidence with weight includes a certified appraiser's report, a sales contract with the settlement statement for a recent purchase and written repair estimates. The Board will not look at evidence shown on a phone or tablet at the hearing and does not make copies for you.

  • If you sign a stipulated value offered by Assessment, your Board appeal is cancelled and you cannot go on to the State Tax Commission.
  • If you skip the stipulation, you keep the hearing, and a loss there can be taken to the State Tax Commission.
  • Commercial appeals to the Commission require a lawyer.
  • Withdrawing an appeal must be in writing from the homeowner and can be done at any time.

Paying the full bill while an appeal is open

Yes, pay it. The county tells owners to pay the printed amount before year end even when a hearing is still ahead. Recalculation of 2026 appeal decisions is suspended until January 2027, and when a lower value is set the excess is refunded automatically.

Paying under protest is optional. Missouri statute 139.031 asks for full payment before the delinquency date plus a written statement of the grounds and the value you claim. The county notes that a protest can slow a refund, since protested money is released only on a set schedule, and that protesting neither protects nor harms your right to appeal. Partial payments are taken for real property, but interest, penalties and fees accrue on whatever is unpaid after December 31, and partial payments cannot be made online.

The 15% residential cap and credit

The county announced a 15% assessment cap for qualifying residential homeowners, tied to a review of the 2023 single-family assessments. Relief comes as a credit on the 2026, 2027 and 2028 bills, spread evenly across those three years. No application is needed, no refund checks go out, and the 2025 bill still had to be paid in full.

The tax money had already been distributed to schools, fire districts, libraries and cities, which is why the relief is a credit and not a check. It covers residential real estate only, not vehicles or boats. Call Assessment if your bill looks wrong rather than assuming a credit has posted.

Senior programs

Two county programs apply to residential property, and an eligible owner may use both. The Senior Property Tax Credit offsets future increases. The Senior Citizen Quad Payment Program lets the owner spread the county bill over four equal installments with no interest or penalties.

  • Both require age 62 or older by December 31 of the relevant year and the home as the only primary residence.
  • The Quad program also requires prior-year taxes to be current, a home assessed solely as residential, and ownership by the person, not a trust.
  • Taxes paid from a mortgage escrow are not eligible for the Quad program.
  • The credit covers ad valorem principal only. Special assessments and CID or TDD charges are due in full.

The state Circuit Breaker credit is a separate program run by the Missouri Department of Revenue at 573-751-3505.

Who owes the tax after a sale

Unpaid real estate tax attaches to the parcel, so the incoming owner answers for any balance. The year's tax is usually split between the two parties, with the buyer credited for the days the seller held title. Normally no money goes to the Collector at the sale itself, though a closing company may pay any amount currently due.

Tell Assessment the new owner and mailing address, because a bill can otherwise go to the seller's old address. When a lender pays from escrow, send the bill on to the lender, and ask the closing company which tax year it is prorating.

If a lien, tenant or repair list is holding up a conventional sale, a cash buyer can close without a lender's appraisal, with the tax paid from your proceeds at closing.

Frequently asked questions

When does Jackson County stop accepting on-time property tax payments?

At the end of December 31. A mailed check must be postmarked by then, and the online system cuts off at 11:40 p.m. Interest, penalties and fees start accruing the next day.

Can I still contest my 2026 Jackson County value?

Not this year. The appeal window closes in mid-July and reopens the next spring. Watch the Board of Equalization's page, and pay the 2026 bill in full by December 31 meanwhile.

Does a refund after a value cut require a protest payment?

No. A lower value triggers an automatic refund, and a protest can slow it down. A protest payment must be on time, in full and accompanied by a written statement.

How is the tax split when a Jackson County home sells midyear?

The buyer owes the full bill by December 31, while the seller's share usually appears as a credit to the buyer at closing. Ask the closing company how your contract divides it.

What address do I use to mail a Jackson County tax payment?

Make it payable to the Jackson County Collector with the property account number on it. Protest payments go to Attention: Protest, P.O. Box 219747, Kansas City, MO 64121-9747. Call 816-881-3232 for the current regular mailing address.

Who to call about a tax question

Tax matters in the county run through Clayton, where three offices share the building at 41 South Central Avenue. One values real estate and personal property (the Assessor). One hears disputes about those values (the Board of Equalization). The third, the Collector of Revenue inside the Department of Revenue, issues bills and receives payment.

St. Louis County tax offices in Clayton
OfficePhoneEmailHours
Assessor, 3rd floor314-615-2555Assessor@stlouiscountymo.govCounter Mon to Thu 8:00 to 3:30; phone Mon to Fri 8:30 to 4:30
Board of Equalization314-615-7195boe@stlouiscountymo.govSame schedule as the Assessor
Collector of Revenue314-615-7100collector@stlouiscountymo.govCounter Mon to Thu 8:00 to 3:30

The Collector bills for more than 200 taxing districts, so two homes in the same city can receive very different totals. Go through the district list on your bill line by line, because each line is a separate taxing body.

The county housing market

No Missouri county is bigger: 1,004,125 people in the 2020 count, and an estimated 990,911 on July 1, 2025 (down 1.4%). Housing runs to 448,637 units and 413,849 households, about 69.2% of them owner-occupied. The typical owned home is worth $276,800, the median rent is $1,209, and the median household makes $82,936. People commute 23.1 minutes on average.

Inside the county are dozens of municipalities and 23 public school districts, among them Rockwood, Parkway, Lindbergh, Mehlville, Pattonville, Ritenour and Ferguson-Florissant. The school levy on a bill can differ a lot between neighbors.

How often homes are reassessed

Missouri law has the County Assessor reassess all real estate countywide in each odd-numbered year, which puts the next round in 2027.

Check the value and property class on a new notice against what you know of the house. If something looks off, phone the Assessor at 314-615-2555 while the appeal window is still open. The Assessor answers value questions by phone on weekdays, while in-person visits run Monday through Thursday.

How to dispute a value

Value disputes go to the Board of Equalization, a body independent of the Assessor. It takes cases from homeowners, businesses and manufacturers, and it also reviews exemption requests from not-for-profit organizations. Contact it at 314-615-7195 or boe@stlouiscountymo.gov.

  • Deadline: under RSMo 137.275 the board must have your appeal by the second Monday in July. That falls on July 12 in 2027.
  • Method: you may appeal in person, through an attorney or agent, or in writing.
  • Burden of proof: RSMo 138.060 gives the assessor's number no presumption of correctness, and in a charter county of more than one million people the assessor has to show the value is no higher than true market value. The board can explain how this applies to you.
  • Next step: the State Tax Commission hears appeals from the board's decision. Ask the board for its current filing instructions.

Evidence for a lower figure can include a recent appraisal, your purchase contract, comparable sales or repair estimates.

Late payment and postmarks

Penalties start after January 1. RSMo 139.100 tells the Collector to charge a penalty on unpaid tax from the day after the first of January, at the rate in RSMo 140.100: 18% of each year's delinquency for land in the back tax book. Land redeemed ahead of a sale cannot be charged more than 2% for each month or part of a month.

A mailed payment is treated as paid on its postmark date, and certified or registered mail counts from the date of registration. With a postmark inside the allowed period, no extra tax or penalty applies. The Collector's page links to a Pay Taxes page, a tax rates lookup and a customer service portal at csportal.stlouiscountymo.gov.

If your bill looks wrong, call 314-615-7100 before you pay, and keep any corrected statement with your closing papers.

Taxes at closing

Every closing in the county touches the tax bill. The title company asks for a payoff or a proration for the current year, and an unpaid earlier year carries the 18% penalty described above. Request your parcel's balance from the Collector and pass that number to the closing agent.

If a lender pays your tax from escrow, confirm that the last bill was paid before you list. If a senior tax freeze is on your account, ask the Collector how it is treated when the property changes hands.

Delinquent parcels go to a county tax sale, which the Collector also runs. With the counter closed Fridays and weekends, a seller who wants a payoff letter that week should call early or pay by mail or online. If you are behind, phone 314-615-7100 for payoff figures and sale dates rather than waiting for a notice.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy St. Louis County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling quickly with tax due

Back tax comes out of your proceeds at closing, so it will not stop a sale. It can slow one if nobody requests the payoff early. Cash buyers do not wait for a lender, which helps if you are working against a deadline. Weigh each offer against what a standard listing would leave after commission and repairs, and see that the settlement statement shows the tax line cleared.

Before you list: a short checklist

  1. Read your parcel's value and property class on the Assessor's notice, and call 314-615-2555 if either looks wrong.
  2. Look at the district lines on your latest bill so you can tell buyers which schools and services come with the address.
  3. Get the parcel's balance from the Collector, older years included, and pay whatever is overdue so the 18% penalty stops growing.
  4. If your lender escrows the tax, confirm the last bill was paid.
  5. If an appeal is on your list, pull together the evidence now.
  6. Hand the payoff figure to the closing agent, and keep the stamped envelope or receipt for any payment you mail.

Settling a delinquent account early is worth the effort, because a buyer's title company will not close until the tax line is clear and the Collector can only confirm a payoff figure during office hours. A seller who handles this a week or two before the closing date avoids a last-minute scramble.

Counter hours in Clayton run only Monday through Thursday, so plan any in-person errand early in the week. Most questions can be handled by phone or email without a trip downtown. When you call, have your parcel number or address ready, plus the bill or notice you are asking about.

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Assessor's counter?

Third floor of 41 South Central Avenue, Clayton, MO 63105. Phones are staffed 8:30 to 4:30 on weekdays, and the counter is open Monday through Thursday, 8:00 to 3:30.

Who hears a value appeal?

The Board of Equalization, reached at 314-615-7195 or boe@stlouiscountymo.gov. It operates apart from the Assessor and takes appeals from homeowners, businesses and manufacturers.

What is the filing cutoff for an appeal?

Missouri statute fixes it at the second Monday of July, which is July 12 in 2027. You may appear yourself, send an agent or attorney, or file in writing.

Do all St. Louis County owners pay the same rate?

No. More than 200 taxing districts appear in the Collector's system, and the ones that cover your parcel set what you owe. A house in one school district can pay differently from a similar house in the next.

Does a postmark on the last day count?

Yes, if it travels by U.S. mail. RSMo 139.100 treats the postmark date as the payment date, and certified or registered mail uses the date of registration. Keep the stamped envelope or receipt.

Clay County housing market

Clay County makes up the northern suburbs of the Kansas City area, with Liberty as the seat and a portion of Kansas City itself inside the line. The 2020 census counted 253,335 residents, and the July 2025 estimate is 265,032. Owners occupy 69.5% of the 110,443 housing units.

  • Middle value of owner-occupied homes, 2020 to 2024: $275,600.
  • Median gross rent: $1,243.
  • Median household income: $88,468.
  • Building permits issued in 2025: 297.

The district names on a statement matter, because every school, library and college district sets its own levy. Two houses with the same assessed value can carry different bills, so check the districts before you quote a tax figure to a buyer.

Where to pay and who to call

Start at claycountymo.tax, where owners search a bill, pay and set up prepayments. Two offices take walk-in business, both open Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

  • Main office: Administration Building, 1 Courthouse Square, Liberty, MO 64068.
  • Clay County Annex: 1901 NE 48th Street, Kansas City, MO 64118.
  • Collector: 816-407-3200. Assessor: 816-407-3500.
  • County Clerk, who takes Board of Equalization forms: 816-407-3570.

The 2026 payment deadline is Wednesday, December 31, 2026. The county follows the state holiday calendar, so offices close at noon on December 24 and stay closed December 25 and 26.

How to contest a Clay County value

The informal hearing is the cheapest place to win. Bring photographs of defects, repair estimates and recent sales of similar houses close to yours. An appraiser at the Assessor's office will look at your evidence and can adjust the number without any board involved. Ask for the decision in writing, and keep the notice with your closing papers in case a buyer asks about the value history.

Talk to the Assessor before you send anything to the Clerk's office. The Board of Equalization can lower a value that sits above true value compared with other properties, and it can also raise one it finds too low. Weigh that risk before you file.

StepWhenHow

Board of Equalization applicationPostmarked or delivered by 5 p.m. on the second Monday in JulyForms go through the County Clerk
Board of Equalization hearingAugustRequests go through the Clerk's office
State Tax Commission appealSeptember 30, or the 30th day after the board's final action if that falls laterFile after the board decides

The July date follows RSMo 137.275, and the commission step follows RSMo 138.430.

If your valuation jumped

Missouri law shifts the burden in one case. Under RSMo 138.060, when an assessed valuation rose at least 15 percent over the previous assessment, other than from new construction or improvement, the Assessor must prove the valuation does not exceed true market value. No presumption exists that the Assessor's figure is correct.

  • Pull the prior and current notices and work out the percentage change.
  • Collect recent sales of similar houses near yours, plus repair estimates for defects the Assessor may not know about.
  • Book the April informal hearing, then decide whether to file with the board by the July deadline.

New residents should know that assessments follow where you lived and what you owned on January 1. The Assessor's office handles people arriving from another county or state, and the Collector's site says to bring the previous county's personal property tax receipt to the DMV.

The August tax sale

Unpaid real estate tax ends up in an online auction run through GovEase, starting at 10:00 a.m. on the fourth Monday of August. The process builds through the spring. In 2026, fees of $135 were added to bills still delinquent in early May and $115 more on June 1, and the last day to pay by card, personal check or online came in mid-June. After that, a property headed to sale needs cash, a cashier's check or a money order.

  • Owners of land that sold the year before can redeem with funds received in person at the Liberty office by 5:00 p.m. on the day after the sale opens. Postmarks and drop box payments do not count.
  • After that, redemption continues until an investor claims a deed.
  • Land that fails to sell after the third offering becomes available over the counter in September.
  • Overbid money is held for the person legally entitled to it. Homeowners and recorded lienholders have 90 days after the deed is claimed to apply, and after 91 days it passes to the county school fund.

The Collector does not partner with or endorse Title Bridge and will not accept due diligence performed by that firm. Only due diligence approved by the Collector's office counts toward a Collector's deed and a redemption. For the 2027 schedule, call 816-407-3200.

Selling with taxes owed

Before you list, ask the Collector for the current balance and let the title company pay it from your proceeds. Delinquent tax follows the land, and a parcel that reaches the August auction can end with someone else holding a deed.

A simple order of work helps. Look up your bill on claycountymo.tax and note the districts and any open balance. Call the Collector at 816-407-3200 to confirm the payoff, since fees can be added to a bill that is still delinquent in spring. Give the title company that figure so it appears on the settlement statement. Once the deed is recorded, make sure the Collector and Assessor have the buyer's name and mailing address, so the next statement is not sent to you.

A cash sale skips the lender's demand that every tax line be clear before funding, though the closing agent still pays what is owed from the price. That can matter if the house has sat delinquent into the spring, when added fees and the online auction timetable start to apply. Cash Home Buyers works with owners in that spot and with inherited or tenant-occupied houses.

If you moved here recently, remember that assessment depends on where you lived and what you owned on January 1. Call the Assessor at 816-407-3500 if you came from another Missouri county or from out of state.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Clay County property tax due date for 2026?

Wednesday, December 31, 2026. Offices are closed December 25 and 26 and open again after that. Pay at the Liberty courthouse, at the Annex on NE 48th Street in Kansas City, or through claycountymo.tax.

Who do I call to dispute my assessment?

Call the Assessor at 816-407-3500 and ask for an informal hearing, which is held in April with an appraiser. If that does not settle it, the County Clerk at 816-407-3570 handles Board of Equalization forms, and the application is due by 5 p.m. on the second Monday in July.

Can the Board of Equalization raise my value?

Yes. The board can lower a value that exceeds true value compared with other properties, and it can raise a value it finds too low. Bring comparable sales that support your number.

When is the tax sale?

It is held online through GovEase on the fourth Monday of August, starting at 10:00 a.m. Call 816-407-3200 for the next schedule, and for redemption or overbid questions.

Do I owe Clay County tax if I just moved here?

Assessment depends on where you lived and what you owned on January 1. A person who moved in from another Missouri county or from out of state should call the Assessor at 816-407-3500. Use the personal property tax receipt from the earlier county when you register a vehicle.

Boone County offices and where to pay

Two county offices matter here. The Assessor sets the value of each parcel. The Collector sends the bill and takes your payment, at Room 118 in the Boone County Government Center (southwest corner, Ninth and Ash, Columbia). Call (573) 886-4285 or come by between 8:00 AM and 5:00 PM on weekdays.

Boone County housing market

When a Boone County bill must be paid

You owe the bill when you get it, and the hard stop is December 31. Statements go out through November. Nothing in the mail by December 10? Call the office, since a lost envelope doesn't wipe out the tax or the penalties.

Mailed checks count as on time if postmarked by December 31, per RSMo 139.100. Street mailboxes sometimes get stamped the next day, so send it several days early. In person, a drop box under the shelter at the Ninth Street entrance accepts payments until midnight on New Year's Eve.

Starting in January, late charges climb monthly until the account is clear. A parcel entered in the back tax book picks up an 18 percent charge on that year's delinquency under RSMo 140.100, or up to 2 percent a month if the owner redeems before the sale.

Boone County tax calendar

The cycle repeats every year. Miss an appeal window and you wait for next year's notices.

What to do if your assessment looks too high

Appeals climb three steps, one at a time.

  • Call the Assessor the day your notice arrives. A brief informal meeting explains how the value was built and clears up many disputes.
  • Not settled? Fill out the Board of Equalization appeal form and mail it to the County Clerk, postmarked no later than July's second Monday unless the board moves the date.
  • Carry the board's ruling to the Missouri State Tax Commission by September 30, or a month after the decision letter if that is later.

The right to that last step comes from RSMo 138.430. Paying under protest is another option: write "paid under protest" on a check for the full bill before year's end, then give the Collector a written statement of the market value you claim. Once the appeal window closes, your only recourse is next year's number.

Preparing for an informal hearing

Informal hearings run from late April to mid June, so use that stretch well. Gather what shows your home's condition as of January 1: photos of damage, repair estimates, and any recent sale or appraisal figures for similar houses nearby. Ask the Assessor staff to walk through the property record, because an error in square footage, age or finish level is the easiest thing to fix.

Write down the market value you think is fair. You'll need that number if you later file with the Board of Equalization or pay under protest. Bring your notice, since the value and parcel details printed on it are what staff will pull up.

Monthly installment plan

A plan from the Collector covers real estate taxes and Neighborhood Improvement District assessments, though you have to pay the current bill before joining. Each month's amount comes from last year's base tax divided by the months remaining, so a plan that begins in March spreads the base across ten payments.

December's installment is adjusted to the real bill. The balance must be gone by December 31, or the plan can end and late fees start. Payment options are a coupon with cash, check or money order, bank debit on the 5th or 20th, or credit card on the 20th with 2.3 percent added.

Escrowed taxes

If your lender folds tax money into the mortgage payment, the lender asks for the bill and pays it. When that request arrives before October 1, you receive an informational statement noting that the lien holder asked for it. A statement lacking that note belongs with your mortgage company right away.

You still carry the responsibility. Penalties begin after December 31 even if a servicer was supposed to pay, so after a servicer change or a loan payoff, confirm where the bill went. With no escrow, pay straight from the informational statement.

Who owes the tax after a sale closes?

Whoever buys the property inherits an unpaid balance, since the tax is a lien on the real estate. The buyer pays the full bill by December 31, the two sides typically prorate by months or days owned, and no tax money changes hands with the Collector at closing.

Closings after October 1 need extra care. The bill can still print in the seller's name and go to the old address until the buyer reports the sale to the Collector or Assessor. If a bill for a sold house reaches you, forward the buyer's name and mailing address to the Collector.

Before listing, phone (573) 886-4285 to learn whether an earlier year is open, and pass that balance to the title company. For a sale landing between October 1 and December 31, settle in the contract who pays the bill on arrival and who updates the mailing address. Keep your own copies of paid statements for the years you owned the home.

For back taxes, RSMo 140.150 allows paying delinquent tax, penalty and costs to the Collector at any point before the parcel is sold. A cash buyer faces the same lien rule, and a clean payoff speeds any closing.

Frequently asked questions

What is the last day to pay Boone County property tax?

December 31. Payment received or postmarked by then avoids charges, which build monthly from January. Bills are mailed during November.

Where can I pay in person?

Go to Room 118 in Columbia's Government Center on weekdays. The Ninth Street entrance has a drop box that stays open until midnight on December 31.

Does the county auction tax certificates?

Yes. The annual sale takes place on the fourth Monday of August at 10:00 AM on the courthouse steps and covers real estate with unpaid taxes.

When is the Board of Equalization deadline?

The second Monday of July, unless the board extends it. After that, you wait for next year's notices.

Do I owe the tax if I never received a bill?

Yes. A bill that never came doesn't cancel the tax or the late fees. Call (573) 886-4285 if December 10 passes with nothing in the mailbox.

Cape Girardeau County at a glance

Cape Girardeau County sits on the Mississippi River in the southeast corner of the state. Cape Girardeau is its biggest city and Jackson holds the courthouse. The July 2025 estimate puts the population at 83,999. Owners live in 66.8% of the homes, so about one house in three is a rental, and many local sellers are landlords with tenants. Their tax bills follow the same rules as everyone else's.

Buyers shop by school district, and that also shapes the levy on a bill. Jackson R-II, Cape Girardeau Public Schools No. 63, Delta R-V, Oak Ridge R-VI and Nell Holcomb R-IV all reach into the county. Look at the district printed on your statement to see which one you pay.

Who handles property tax

Four offices matter here. Three of them share the Jackson administration building at One Barton Square, and the Collector also runs a branch in the city of Cape Girardeau.

  • Assessor: 1 Barton Square, Suite 201, Jackson, 573-243-2468. Appraisal questions can go to appraisal@capecounty.us.
  • Collector: Suite 303 in Jackson, 573-243-4476, and 2311 Bloomfield Road, Suite 102, Cape Girardeau, 573-335-2606. Hours are 8:00 to 4:30 on weekdays.
  • County Clerk: 100 Court Street, Suite 301, Jackson. Appeal forms go here.
  • Recorder of Deeds: Suite 203, 573-243-8123.

Don't confuse the Treasurer (100 Court Street, Suite 202) with the Collector. The Treasurer does not take tax payments. A house inside the limits of Cape Girardeau or Jackson gets new-address requests through that city's planning office instead of the Assessor.

How to pay your tax bill

A statement is payable the day you receive it. The county treats December 31 as the final day free of late charges. Choose from these ways to pay.

  • Walk in to either Collector office and hand over cash, a check, a money order, a cashier's check or a card.
  • Use the drop boxes at the Jackson front door and south lot, or the door slot at the Bloomfield Road office.
  • By mail to One Barton Square, Suite 303, Jackson, postmarked by the end of the month you are paying in.
  • Pay online or call 1-877-690-3729 and enter jurisdiction code 3516. A service fee is added either way.

If a title company or lender needs proof of payment today, pay at the counter. An online or phone confirmation is only a confirmation, and the paid receipt follows after several days. Credit cards no longer work by phone or mail. Bills and receipts can be searched and printed from the county's tax portal by owner, parcel number or address.

How to appeal your assessment

Values are reset for January 1 of each odd-numbered year under RSMo 137.115, and new buildings or additions are picked up when completed. Talk to the Assessor first. A formal appeal then moves through three stages.

  1. Informal hearing: call 573-243-3123 ahead of the second Monday in July.
  2. Board of Equalization: sessions start the third Monday in July, and the County Clerk must have your signed form before the second Monday.
  3. State Tax Commission: the deadline is September 30, or 30 days after the Board decides if that is later.

The county wants proof that the January 1 value is off. Good evidence includes an appraisal from a Missouri appraiser, a broker opinion of value no more than three years old, an arm's-length sales contract from the past year, or repair and construction cost records. Foreclosure sales, tax sales and sales between relatives do not count as market evidence. Corporations, LLCs and partnerships file through an authorized agent, and at the State Tax Commission they need an attorney.

Homestead tax credits

Voters passed two credits on April 7, 2026 that cap increases on the home you live in. Proposition A is a senior credit for owners 62 and older under SB 190 and SB 756. Proposition B is a general homestead credit under SB 3 for any owner who lives in the home.

  • Own the house, live in it and be the person who owes the tax.
  • Rentals, commercial parcels and farmland are left out.
  • Any delinquent tax, interest or penalty disqualifies you.
  • Applications are taken February 1 through April 15, and the 2027 cutoff is April 15, 2027.

You see the credit as a reduction on the November statement, not as a check. It stays with the owner and the house. When title transfers it ends, so you lose it at closing and your buyer must apply fresh. Ask about it at homestead@capecounty.us or 573-987-5010. The state statute is RSMo 137.1050. A different program, the Missouri Property Tax Credit claim, uses Form 948 signed by the Assessor.

Delinquent taxes and the August tax sale

The county auctions delinquent land on the fourth Monday of August (RSMo 140.150). Recent auctions started at 10:00 a.m. on the Administration Building's third floor, and the next is in August 2027. The parcel list is posted on the Collector's page and gets shorter as owners pay.

Before listing a parcel, the Collector mails the record owner a first-class notice, and adds a certified-mail notice when assessed value tops $1,000. Never getting the letter does not wipe out the debt. If your land sold in 2025, phone 573-243-4476 and ask the Collector to figure the redemption amount for a specific date.

A penalty starts on any tax left unpaid after January 1. Once land is on the back tax book, RSMo 140.100 sets interest at 18 percent per year of delinquency. Until the moment of sale, you can clear the account by paying the Collector the back tax plus penalty, interest and costs.

Selling with taxes and recording a deed

Start by looking up your parcel on the Collector's portal and the Assessor's real estate search. Check that the owner name is right and see whether a balance is open. Any amount owed can come out of your sale proceeds at closing through the title company, which matters because the tax sticks to the land, not the person.

The Recorder's office in Jackson files the deed. Recording and marriage license fees rose $2 on August 28, 2026, and the fee on a document is split among county and state funds. Phone 573-243-8123 for today's deed fee so your closing check is correct.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay property tax in Cape Girardeau County?

At the Collector's offices in Jackson (One Barton Square, Suite 303) or Cape Girardeau (2311 Bloomfield Road, Suite 102), in a drop box, by mail, online or by phone. Call 573-243-4476 or 573-335-2606 with questions.

What is the due date for real estate tax?

Bills are due on receipt, and December 31 is the last day before late charges. A mailed payment needs a postmark no later than the end of the month you are paying in.

How late can I appeal an assessment?

Get signed forms to the County Clerk before the second Monday in July. Hearings begin the third Monday, and a State Tax Commission appeal is due September 30 or 30 days after the Board rules, whichever comes later.

Did the county pass a homestead tax credit?

Yes. Voters approved a senior credit and a general homestead credit on April 7, 2026. Applications for 2027 open February 1 and close April 15, 2027, and delinquent taxes disqualify an applicant.

Does the tax credit transfer when I sell?

No. The credit is tied to the primary residence and the owner who applied, so it does not move to a new home or a new owner. A buyer who qualifies must apply separately.

Greene County offices and contacts

Springfield-area tax bills pass through three desks. The Assessor sets the value. The County Clerk staffs the appeals board and compiles the yearly tax book from those values and the levies voters approved. The Collector of Revenue mails statements and receives the money.

  • Collector of Revenue: (417) 868-4036, open weekdays from 8:00 with no lunch closure
  • Assessor: 940 N Boonville Ave, Room 35, Springfield, (417) 868-4101 for real estate and (417) 868-4195 for personal property
  • County Clerk and Board of Equalization: 940 North Boonville, Springfield, MO 65802

The Assessor opens at 8:00 most weekdays and at 8:30 on Wednesday. Both offices close at 4:30. Owners can look up statements and receipts on the Collector's site. The processor, not the county, charges 1.5 percent on debit cards and 2.3 percent on credit cards (with a $2 minimum), or $1 for an e-check.

An online payment posts to your account within about three hours, and no receipt is emailed. If you need proof the same day, for instance at a closing, pay at the counter.

Greene County housing snapshot

Greene County lies in the Ozark foothills of southwest Missouri, anchored by Springfield. Other cities are Ash Grove, Battlefield, Fair Grove, Republic, Rogersville, Strafford, Walnut Grove and Willard. About 309,286 people live here in 142,405 housing units, and owners occupy 57.5 percent of them. The middle owned home sells on paper for $221,300, while gross rent has a median of $989. In 2025 the county issued 966 building permits.

How the Assessor reaches a value

The Assessor is elected to a four-year term and has held the office since 2021. Each taxable parcel is listed and assessed yearly, with January 1 as the reference date. The office also keeps the tax map, and when warranty deeds arrive from the Recorder it redraws lot lines, so a split or combined lot shows up once the deed is on record.

Residential property is assessed at 19 percent under RSMo 137.115. Fresh values land in odd years, 2027 being the next, and a house that rises more than 15 percent needs an on-site inspection behind it.

The Assessor's Public Access website updates every night and shows the address, owner, taxing district, school district, section, township and range, plus map layers for lots, fire districts and city limits. Use it to confirm your taxing districts before you compare your bill with a neighbor's.

How to appeal your assessment

The Clerk lays out three steps. Step one, a chat with an appraiser, is optional, and you can file a formal appeal without it.

Greene County real estate appeal path
StepWhereDeadline
Informal talk with an appraiserAssessor, (417) 868-4101As soon as the notice arrives
Formal appealCounty Clerk, 940 North BoonvilleSecond Monday in July
State appealMissouri State Tax CommissionSeptember 30, or a month after the Board rules if that is later

Eight citizens sit on the Board of Equalization, three appointed by the County Commission and five by the City of Springfield. Monthly, on the second Tuesday at 9:00 a.m. at 1126 N Boonville, they certify tax book corrections, and in July they hear formal appeals. At the hearing the Assessor presents the evidence behind the value, and you answer with your own. The Board may raise the figure, lower it or leave it alone.

Senior tax credit and freeze

Qualifying seniors can apply to the Collector for a Senior Tax Credit, which holds a real estate tax bill steady in future years. The application window is January 1 through June 30.

As of January 1, 2026, the Collector no longer requires annual renewal. Credit holders must report a change in ownership or occupancy within 45 days and answer any audit request within 45 days. Remote applicants need a copy of a government photo ID showing the date of birth.

A seller whose house carries the credit should tell the Collector about the sale inside those 45 days and ask what becomes of the credit when the title changes hands.

When taxes go unpaid

Any bill open on January 1 draws the 18 percent penalty of RSMo 140.100. A mailed payment is dated by its postmark.

An owner contesting a value can pay in full before the delinquency date and file a written statement with the Collector naming the grounds and the value claimed. RSMo 139.031 then requires a suit against the Collector within 90 days. The State Tax Commission adds that an appeal can be filed before the bill is paid, but penalty and interest still apply if the bill is late.

Land with unpaid years can be offered at the August tax sale once the owner of record has been notified by mail, and the owner can still pay off the balance before the sale. Call the Collector at (417) 868-4036 for current figures.

What to have ready before you list

Collect four things before the sign goes up: the current statement from the Collector, any notice of changed value from the Assessor, the parcel number and the legal description of the lot. The first two answer a buyer's questions about taxes, and the last two let a title company move fast.

Weekday timing helps too. The Collector's counter is open from 8:00 to 4:30 and the Assessor's from 8:00 (8:30 on Wednesday), so a morning visit to Springfield can settle questions at both before a closing.

If you disagree with a value, remember the order of events. Talk to an appraiser, take it to the Board if needed, and pay the bill on time while the appeal is open, because the State Tax Commission says late payment still draws penalty and interest.

Selling a Greene County house with taxes in play

Find the parcel on the Collector's statements and receipts page and print the balance for the title company. Buyers ask about school and fire districts, so check those on the Public Access map. Also tell the Collector about the sale if a senior credit is on the house.

Your sales contract says how the current year is split with the buyer, and the title company normally pays the Collector out of your proceeds. Give it the parcel number so the payoff lines up with county records. Prior-year balances matter most, since a clean current bill does not help if an older year is still open. If you are unsure which tax year is being prorated, ask before you sign.

If you hold a vacant inherited home, a house with a long tenant lease or one that needs a new roof, a written cash offer is an option. Taxes get paid from the price at closing, and nobody waits on a lender's appraisal.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay Greene County property tax?

Online or at the Collector of Revenue's counter, and (417) 868-4036 answers questions. Closing time is 4:30 p.m. on weekdays. Cards and e-checks add a processor fee, and online receipts post in roughly three hours.

What is the Greene County appeal deadline?

Each year the form must reach the County Clerk by the second Monday in July.

Do I have to see the Assessor before filing an appeal?

No, but many owners call (417) 868-4101 first because concerns often get settled there. The informal meeting is not a required step.

Can a Greene County senior freeze property tax?

Yes, with the Collector's Senior Tax Credit. Apply between January 1 and June 30. You no longer renew each year, but report ownership or occupancy changes within 45 days.

Who sits on the Greene County Board of Equalization?

Eight taxpayers: the County Commission appoints three, and Springfield appoints five. The Clerk acts as secretary without a vote.

Who values, bills and collects the tax

An elected Assessor and an elected Collector divide the duties. The Assessor determines what each parcel is worth. The Collector sends out one combined bill and distributes what comes in to schools, fire districts and the rest. You will find both downtown in the Administration Building, 201 N. Second Street, weekdays 8 to 5.

  • Assessor: 636-949-7425 for real estate values, 636-949-7428 for informal hearings outside a reassessment year, 636-949-7420 for personal property.
  • Collector of Revenue: Suite 134, 636-949-7470.
  • Online payments: stcharlesmocollector.org.

Rates are out of both offices' hands. Each taxing body picks its own levy, and about 3% of the money collected stays with county government. A parcel sits inside at least six jurisdictions: state, county, school district, fire district, ambulance district and library. That is why identical houses in different corners of the county can owe different amounts.

The county market in brief

The county spans 593 square miles in east central Missouri. St. Charles is the seat and O'Fallon the largest city. About 426,499 residents share 174,278 housing units, and four of every five homes (80.5%) are owner-occupied. A typical owned home is worth $320,800. The median household earns $104,692, median rent is $1,370, and the average commute is 24.5 minutes.

Growth followed the highways: Interstate 70 across the middle, Interstate 64 in the southwest, and Routes 364 and 370 toward St. Louis County. The area between I-70, I-64 and Route 94 is now called the Westplex. High schools sort into five districts (Fort Zumwalt, Francis Howell, Orchard Farm, St. Charles and Wentzville), and each district puts its own line on the bill.

How a home is valued

For each property, the Assessor estimates the price it would bring on the open market on the tax date. Odd-numbered years bring a full revaluation of real estate. New construction joins the rolls yearly, and vehicles and other personal property are assessed annually.

The estimate draws on several kinds of data:

  • Property type: residential, commercial, industrial or agricultural.
  • Structure measurements, checked against building permits and aerial photography.
  • Location data such as zoning, road access and neighborhood.
  • Comparable recent sales, minus any far above or below normal market value.

An assessment is a mass appraisal built on statistics for groups of similar homes. It is different from a sale price, which is what a buyer actually paid, and from an appraisal, which is one detailed opinion of a single property made for a private purpose. If your value moved although you changed nothing, the market for similar homes is usually the cause. Notices go out each April, and the Assessor's website has a property database for finding your parcel.

Payment dates and methods

Real estate and personal property statements are issued by December 1 and are payable through December 31. Money that arrives in January picks up the penalty and interest shown on the statement. Not receiving the bill is no defense.

  • In person at the first-floor payment windows or the drop boxes at 201 N. Second Street. Cash goes to the windows only. Checks, money orders and cashier's checks can go in the drop boxes.
  • By mail to the Collector at Room 134. Mailed payments count as of the postmark, and cash should never be mailed.
  • By phone on the toll-free tax payment line, 1-855-227-7840, with the bill number ready.
  • Online at stcharlesmocollector.org. If you use your own bank's bill pay, start it at least five working days before December 31.

If you cannot pay the whole bill, partial payments made before December 31 reduce the late interest and penalty that would otherwise apply. The Collector also takes advance payments during the year. Lenders and tax services get an electronic file for escrow accounts, but the owner is still on the hook for the full amount.

How to appeal your assessment

An appeal has three steps in a fixed order. Skip the Board of Equalization and the State Tax Commission will not hear you. So start with the informal hearing, then the Board, then the Commission.

  1. Informal hearing with Assessor staff, offered from the end of April through early June. The notice asks you to book within 10 days of its mailing date. Bring whatever supports your number: a recent sales contract, an appraiser's report, comparable sales, photos of defects.
  2. Board of Equalization. Your form has to be in the Registrar's hands by 5 p.m. on the second Monday of July, which will be July 12, 2027. Cases are heard in July and August.
  3. State Tax Commission. The filing date is September 30, or 30 days after the board decides if that comes later. Buyers who closed after the second Monday in June have until December 31.

Be careful with companies that charge a fee to dispute a value. The data they use is public, and the Assessor's office provides it free.

Senior tax relief

The Collector's Senior Real Estate Property Tax Relief Program covers the primary home of residents who were 62 or older and living there on January 1 of the tax year. The credit has to be applied for or renewed annually.

The program began with tax year 2024 and works as a credit against future increases. Someone who becomes eligible on January 1, 2026 sets the base year with the November 2026 bill and should not expect a reduction on that bill. The credit covers every taxing jurisdiction on the bill, including schools and fire districts, but it excludes bond debt levies and the State Blind Pension Fund. Only real estate qualifies, so a mobile home taxed as personal property does not. Ask the Collector at 636-949-7470 when the next application window opens.

Who owes the tax when a house sells

The owner of record when the tax year ends owes that year's bill. The title company normally prorates the year between you and the buyer at closing, and the buyer writes the whole check in December.

Look up your parcel in the Assessor's database before listing and set its value beside recent sales nearby. A value that seems high, with the July deadline still ahead, is a reason to use the appeal steps above. Back tax is a bigger worry: the Collector runs the county tax sale every August, so settle any delinquency well ahead of it. Get a current payoff figure from the Collector and hand it to the closing agent.

Which office answers questions about a St. Charles County bill?

Can a St. Charles County bill be paid in pieces?

Yes, you can pay part of it before December 31, which reduces the late interest and penalty that would otherwise build up. The Collector issues a receipt each time. Advance payments toward a future bill are also accepted.

When does St. Charles County reassess next?

Missouri law calls for a fresh valuation of real estate in odd-numbered years, which makes 2027 the next one. Notices come in April, with informal hearings from the end of April to early June.

What if I miss the Board of Equalization deadline?

Usually your appeal for that year is over, and a State Tax Commission appeal is blocked too unless you just bought the property. The cutoff is 5 p.m. on the second Monday of July, July 12 in 2027.

Who covers the tax share at a St. Charles County closing?

Both of you, for your share of the year. Taxes are often prorated at closing, and the buyer then pays the whole bill at year end. Ask your title company for the proration worksheet before you sign.

How Randolph County taxes a house

One office values each parcel, the Assessor, and another mails the bill, the Collector. Both offices are in the courthouse in Huntsville. Values are fixed on January 1, statements follow in autumn, and the full amount has to reach the Collector before the year ends.

Randolph County is in north-central Missouri, with Huntsville as the seat and Moberly as the largest city. Population is about 24,513, with a typical owned home worth $159,300 and 71.4 percent of households owning. Median gross rent is $760.

The school district printed on your statement drives much of the bill. Houses fall in Moberly, Westran R-I at Huntsville, Higbee R-VIII, Northeast Randolph County R-IV at Cairo or Renick R-V, and each district has its own levy. Check that line before comparing two Randolph County addresses. The Collector can tell you which district a parcel sits in if the statement is unclear. Moberly also has a community college and a Bible college, so rental demand near campus can differ from the rural townships.

Offices and contacts

Every county office is in the courthouse at 372 Hwy. JJ, Huntsville, MO 65259. Weekday hours generally run eight to four. The main number is 844-277-6555, and each office has its own extension. The county home page links to the Collector's site and to the Assessor's property search.

  • Collector: Suite 1G, extension 310. This office takes in current and back tax and passes it to the schools, cities, library, ambulance and fire districts.
  • Assessor: sets values and changes mailing addresses. Parcel records are searchable from the county home page.
  • County Clerk: the place to ask for equalization board forms and dates.
  • County Commission: meets Tuesdays and Wednesdays at 9 a.m., with agendas on the county site.

Mortgage companies also call the Collector for tax figures or to pay from escrow. Bills are posted online, so if yours is missing from the Collector's search, check with the Assessor.

What share of your home's value is taxed

The Assessor starts from market value and taxes only a slice of it. RSMo 137.115 sets that slice at nineteen percent for houses, twelve percent for farmland and thirty-two percent for commercial parcels.

Revaluation happens in odd years, using the January 1 date, and the figure carries into the following even year unless a building is added. The next reset is January 1, 2027. When a house's value jumps more than fifteen percent for reasons other than new construction, the statute calls for an on-site inspection, and the owner can ask that the inside be viewed as well.

Each district on your bill then applies its own levy to that assessed figure. Two houses of equal value can therefore owe different amounts.

Due date and ways to pay

The deadline is the last day of December. Payments are accepted inside the courthouse, by mail, in the front drop box, at the drive-up window, and online by Discover, MasterCard or Visa. The online convenience fee goes to the card processor, and the county shows the amount before you confirm.

A mailed check counts on its postmark. RSMo 139.100 treats mail as paid on the date stamped on the envelope, and a postal delay brings no penalty when the postmaster verifies it in writing. Once January arrives, the penalty in RSMo 140.100 applies: eighteen percent of the year's delinquency on land in the back tax book, capped at two percent a month on land redeemed before a sale.

Appealing a value that looks too high

Talk to the Assessor first, take the matter to the equalization board next and then, if needed, to the State Tax Commission. Phone the Assessor's office when the notice lands, ask how they arrived at the number, and show proof of market value.

When that conversation fails, ask the County Clerk for the equalization board's forms and filing dates. Under RSMo 138.060 the board decides appeals in a summary way, and no presumption favors the Assessor's number. Going further means a complaint to the State Tax Commission (RSMo 138.430). That one is due September 30, or thirty days after the board finishes if that comes later.

Evidence outweighs frustration with the bill. Saying taxes are too high is not relevant testimony, while a recent sale, photographs or an appraiser's opinion are. An owner who wants to protest the tax itself pays the whole bill before the delinquency date and files a written statement with the Collector, then has ninety days to file suit under RSMo 139.031.

Selling a Randolph County house

Before signing a sales contract, find out your balance from the Collector. The closing agent will then split the year's tax between you and the buyer. Because the assessment date is January 1, the bill stays with the parcel when ownership changes midyear.

A few habits keep a sale from stalling over tax:

  • Get a written statement of current and any delinquent amounts from Suite 1G.
  • Hand the title company the parcel number from the Assessor's record.
  • Once closed, give both offices the new owner's mailing address.
  • Where a lender pays from escrow, confirm the payment posted before you list.

Selling with back taxes or an estate house

Owners with back taxes, an estate house or a vacant property in Moberly, Huntsville or one of the villages sometimes choose a cash sale to close within weeks. That buyer needs the same payoff numbers a traditional buyer does, so the Collector's statement is the first paper to request whichever route you take. Bring the parcel number, and expect to wait a day or two for a written payoff.

With cash there is no lender approval and no bank appraisal to wait on, and those two steps are where houses with tax or title questions tend to stall. The title company searches for liens, pays the county from your proceeds, and records the deed as usual. Get the payoff in writing before accepting an offer, and ask which costs land on the buyer and which on you.

Frequently asked questions

Where can I pay my Randolph County tax bill?

At the Collector's office, courthouse Suite 1G, 372 Hwy. JJ in Huntsville, or by mail, drop box, drive-up window or online. Weekday hours are 8 a.m. through 4 p.m., and the phone is 844-277-6555 extension 310.

When does Randolph County property tax become late?

After December 31. A mailed payment is on time if its postmark is that date or earlier. Penalties under RSMo 140.100 begin once January arrives.

What portion of my home's value is taxed in Randolph County?

Nineteen percent for residential property under RSMo 137.115, against twelve for farmland and thirty-two for commercial parcels. The levy for your school and taxing districts is then applied to that assessed figure.

How often are Randolph County homes revalued?

Every other year. The Assessor sets new values as of January 1 of odd-numbered years, so the next general valuation is January 1, 2027, and it generally stays in force through 2028 unless the house is improved.

Is it too late to dispute a value if the board date passed?

Maybe not. A State Tax Commission complaint is due September 30 or thirty days after the board finishes, whichever falls later, so a late board date can still leave room. Call the County Clerk right away for the board's dates.

Camden County at a glance

Camden County is the Lake of the Ozarks county in central Missouri, and Camdenton is the seat. Osage Beach is the largest city. The county's own site is camdencountymo.gov. Population was 42,745 in 2020, and the 2025 estimate is 44,047.

The incorporated places are Camdenton, Lake Ozark, Linn Creek, Osage Beach and Richland. Camdenton R-III, Climax Springs R-IV, Macks Creek R-V and Stoutland R-II are the main school districts. A house near the water in Osage Beach can sit in a different tax picture from one in Stoutland, because each school, fire or library district adds its own levy to the bill. Who handles property tax in Camden County

Three offices in Camdenton share the work, and the county phone line is 573-346-4440 with an extension for each.

  • The Assessor values real and personal property as of January 1. Real estate and GIS are at 50 Roofener Street, and personal property is at 1 Court Circle NW, Suite 6. The extension is 1260.

How to appeal your assessment

You work through four steps, and the first costs nothing. State law reassesses every parcel in odd-numbered years, so the next full cycle falls in 2027, and owners whose value rose get a Change in Assessment Notice with the appeal rights printed on it.

  1. Informal appeal: call the Assessor at 573-317-3865 or 573-317-3896 (condominiums at 573-317-3838). Informal hearings usually run in April and May.
  2. Board of Equalization: a three-member panel of local taxpayers appointed by the County Commission meets in July. Book through the County Clerk, and file on or before the second Monday of July.
  3. State Tax Commission: file by September 30 or 30 days after the Board's decision, whichever is later. The commission's phone is 573-751-2414.
  4. Circuit court: at this level an attorney is expected.

The Board rules on fair market value alone. Come with comparable sales or an appraisal, and skip any complaint that the tax rate is too high. RSMo 138.430 gives the appeal rights to the State Tax Commission, and RSMo 137.275 sets the July cutoff.

If Camden County property tax goes unpaid

January 1 is the line. Under RSMo 139.100 the Collector adds a penalty to taxes unpaid after the first of January, and a postmark by the due date counts as timely. Land that reaches the back tax book carries an 18 percent penalty on each year's delinquency, or up to two percent per month if it is redeemed before the sale, under RSMo 140.100.

If you dispute a bill, pay all of it before the delinquency date and attach a written protest. The Collector sets the contested portion aside, and you then have ninety days to sue the Collector in circuit court (RSMo 139.031).

The county's next tax sale is announced for Monday, August 23, 2027 at 10:00 a.m. State law holds it on the fourth Monday in August (RSMo 140.150). Only Missouri residents may bid, and they must be at the courthouse by 8:30 and registered at the Collector's Office first. A parcel offered at a "fourth sale" must be placed on hold in the Collector's Office for at least 150 days.

Senior property tax freeze

The Assessor administers the SB 190 senior credit for people 62 and older. The 2027 sign-up window opens January 4, 2027 and ends June 30, 2027.

  • You must hold the deed and owe the annual tax bill.
  • The property can't be titled to an LLC or a corporation. Revocable or living trusts are accepted if you are named trustee.

The freeze holds the assessed portion of the bill at the amount paid in the base year, and new construction can remove it. The state statute behind it is RSMo 137.1050. The credit follows the owner and the primary residence, so a sale ends it for the seller, and a buyer applies on their own.

If the parcel still has a balance, the title company pays the Collector out of your proceeds, and the settlement statement divides the year's tax between you and the buyer. Check the collector portal before you list, because a lien on the parcel affects how fast a deal can close.

Deeds are recorded at the Recorder's office, 1 Court Circle NW in Camdenton, 573-346-4440 extension 1300. Fees effective August 28, 2026 are $26 for the first page of a deed and $3 for each added page, with an extra $25 if the document isn't on 8.5 by 11 paper with a three-inch top margin. Land record searches use the Recorder's iCounty site at camdenmo.icounty.com.

  2. Call extension 1260 if the value or owner details look wrong, and extension 1200 for payment questions.

Pay the Collector at 1 Court Circle NW, Suite 4, Camdenton, or use the taxpayer portal at collector.camdencountymo.gov. Call 573-346-4440 extension 1200 with any question about a statement.

When is the Camden County Board of Equalization deadline?

Appeals must be filed on or before the second Monday in July, with the appointment set through the County Clerk at extension 1220. The Board meets during July.

Does Camden County have a senior tax freeze?

Yes, the SB 190 freeze for owners 62 and older. The 2027 application period runs January 4 through June 30, 2027 at the Assessor's real estate office, 50 Roofener Street, Camdenton.

The next sale is Monday, August 23, 2027 at 10:00 a.m. Bidders must be Missouri residents and register at the Collector's Office before the sale.

More than 70,000 real estate parcels. Reassessment happens in odd-numbered years, with new construction added when it is finished.

Who to call about your bill

Value and billing live in different offices here. The rule is simple: the Assessor decides what the parcel is worth, and the Collector mails the statement and cashes the check. You can reach both at the Carthage courthouse, 302 S. Main. The Collector keeps a second counter at the Joplin Courts Building, 633 S. Pearl.

  • Carthage Collector: 417-358-0409 (personal property) or 417-358-0411 (real property), Room 107
  • Joplin Collector: 417-625-4324, either kind of tax

  • Assessor for personal property: 417-358-0437

Walk-in service is 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays. The Assessor observes state holidays and works those same hours.

Housing in Jasper County

The county occupies the far southwest corner of Missouri, bordering Kansas, with Carthage as its seat. Joplin is the biggest city and spills slightly into Newton County. As of July 1, 2025 the county held 127,428 people and 56,504 housing units. Owners live in 62.8% of the homes, and the median owner-occupied value is $166,900.

Each town, school district and fire district sets its own levy, but they all land on a single county statement. Before you list, look at your last bill to see which districts your address belongs to, because buyers tend to ask. A Joplin address can also fall on the Newton County side of the line, so confirm which county's Collector and Assessor cover your parcel before you send any payment or paperwork.

When are Jasper County property taxes due?

The Collector mails statements during the first week of November. Payment is expected as soon as you receive one, and anything unpaid after December 31 is delinquent. To pay by mail, get a USPS postmark dated 12/31/26 or earlier. The website stops taking payments at 11:59 p.m. on 12/31/26 and reopens in 2027, when interest and penalties apply to whatever came in late. Envelopes postmarked after the deadline are sent back unless the late charges are enclosed.

No statement by the end of November? Phone the Collector at once. The office stresses that an unreceived bill is still a debt. A glitch with the phone line or website will not move the legal date either, so keep the drop box in mind. Both offices have one that works around the clock.

Those service charges go to the payment processor and are separate from your tax. Missouri statute 139.055 puts the cost on the people who choose electronic payment, so a paper check or a trip to the counter costs nothing extra.

Where the Assessor fits in

Whatever the Assessor's file says is what the Collector bills. A wrong mailing address, a bad legal description or a vehicle you no longer own is the Assessor's to correct. For land and buildings, dial 417-358-0440 and ask how the parcel was valued and what the latest notice means.

Personal property follows a separate yearly schedule. Lists go out by mail in early January, and you owe them back by March 1 to avoid a penalty. The PIN on the mailed sheet lets you file online, though emailed lists are refused. Ownership on January 1 sets the tax, even if you sold the car in February. Businesses report furniture and equipment the same way, and anyone renting or leasing space to tenants owes a tenant list by January 30.

One more item: a statement of non-assessment (sometimes called a tax waiver) is good only for licensing a vehicle. You must bring the title or registration into the office yourself.

How to appeal your assessment

Disputes are heard by the county board of equalization. Missouri statute 138.060 tells the board to rule in summary fashion and to start with no assumption that the assessor got the number right. When a value climbed fifteen percent or more over the previous assessment with no new construction or improvement, the same law shifts the burden of proof to the assessor.

Ask the Assessor at 417-358-0440 what this year's filing date and hearing process are. Gather comparable sales, a recent appraisal or your purchase contract before you go. An open appeal does not pause the bill, so pay by December 31 or interest and penalties begin.

Senior tax credit

Older owners can apply for the SB190 Senior Citizen Tax Credit through the Collector, Room 107 of the Carthage courthouse. In the latest cycle, filing began in early February and ended May 31, and applicants could use a QR code or the PIN on a renewal notice to apply online. Check with the Collector for the dates of the next round.

  • Age 62 or older by midnight on December 31 of the first credit year
  • A Jasper County home that is your primary residence
  • Prior-year taxes already paid

Renewing owners file in the same window. Separately, the Missouri Department of Revenue offers a state Property Tax Credit for certain seniors and 100% disabled individuals, at 573-751-3505. The two programs do not depend on each other.

Selling with taxes owed

A few phone calls early on keep a tax balance from slowing your closing.

  1. Get today's balance on the parcel from the Collector before you pick a closing date.
  2. Settle with the escrow or title agent whether the current year is paid off or prorated, and write that into the contract.
  3. If you inherited the house, track down older statements and get the figure for each year before telling a buyer your price.
  4. Once the sale is done, the new owner should give the Assessor a mailing address so the November statement finds them.

Because bills come due on receipt and go delinquent after December 31, a fall closing can leave the current year unpaid for a few weeks. The title company usually pays it out of your proceeds. A cash sale has no lender underwriting to wait on, so the payoff can happen sooner, though the balance is cleared in the same way.

Frequently asked questions

What is the deadline to pay Jasper County property tax?

December 31. A mailed check needs a USPS postmark of 12/31/26 or earlier, and the website closes at 11:59 p.m. that night. Later payments carry interest and penalties.

Where do I pay in Jasper County if I live near Joplin?

Use the Joplin Courts Building at 633 S. Pearl, phone 417-625-4324, so you do not have to drive to Carthage. Each office also has a drop box that is open all day and night.

How much extra does it cost to pay online in Jasper County?

An e-check adds $2.00 and a credit card adds 2.45% of the balance. The county sees none of that money. Paying by check or in person carries no fee.

I did not get my statement. Do I still owe?

Yes. The tax is owed even if no statement arrives, and penalty and interest still build up. Phone the Collector if you have nothing by the end of November.

Who do I call to fix my address or vehicle on the statement?

The Assessor. Dial 417-358-0440 for real estate or 417-358-0437 for personal property. The Collector can only bill what the Assessor's file shows.

Which offices handle property tax in Platte County?

Property tax here touches three county desks. Valuation belongs to the Assessor. Appeals to the Board of Equalization and tax credit applications go through the County Clerk, who also builds the tax book. Bills are mailed and money is taken by the Collector of Revenue.

Find the Collector at 415 3rd St., Room 212 in the Administration Building, Platte City, MO 64079, or call (816) 858-3356. The counter staffs weekdays from 8 to 5. Real estate staff at the Assessor pick up (816) 858-3316 until 4:30. The County Clerk, at (816) 858-3340, fields tax relief questions. Send value, name, address, vehicle and tax waiver questions to the assessor, and missing-statement questions to the collector.

Platte County market snapshot

Platte City is the seat of a Kansas City-area county bounded on the southwest by the Missouri River. The airport lies within its borders, along with Parkville, Weston, Riverside, Dearborn and Smithville. Park Hill, Platte County School District Number 3, North Platte R-I and West Platte County R-II run the schools.

Home values run high. The county grew to an estimated 114,400 people in 2025, a 7.2 percent gain on 2020, and counts 47,969 housing units, 67.4 percent of them owner-occupied. The median owned home is valued at $345,100, rent is $1,334 monthly and household income is $96,227. Builders took out 425 permits in 2025.

When bills are due

Bills go out in November, and the assessor's calendar gives November 1 as the date they leave the Collector. Payment is expected on receipt, and December 31 is the line after which late charges begin. Postmark the envelope by then. Mail stamped later is returned unprocessed unless penalty and interest are added to it.

You still owe the tax if a statement is lost in the mail, and a problem with the phone or web payment system does not stretch the statutory deadline. Read the address and legal description on every bill. No bill by the end of November? Phone the Collector's office at once.

Ways to pay

Payment channels are the counter, the mail, the website, the 1-800 phone number printed on the bill and a 24-hour drop box outside the Platte County Government Complex. At the counter the Collector accepts cash, a personal check, a cashier's check, a money order or a credit or debit card.

After hours, use the drop box. The county is closed November 26 and 27 and December 24 and 25 this year, which affects year-end payments, and the Collector can give its own holiday schedule.

How the 2027 reassessment affects owners

State law calls for a reassessment of all real property every odd-numbered January 1, and the 2027 round in Platte County is underway. The stated goal is equalization rather than extra revenue. Early estimates put about 8,000 parcels on track for a decrease, about 900 for an increase under 1 percent, and just under 13,000 for an increase over 15 percent.

Any parcel projected to climb above 15 percent, new construction aside, receives a written notice plus an inspection of the exterior. The inside is viewed only on the owner's request. Look up your estimated 2027 value on the assessor's Beacon property search, shown next to the 2026 value. Final numbers are set in early 2027 and the estimates can shift.

Assessment rates are 19 percent of market value for residential, 32 percent for commercial and 12 percent for agricultural property.

How to contest a value

The assessor describes a three-stage path, each with its own date: an informal review, then the county board, then the state.

Platte County real property appeal steps
StepWhereTiming
Informal hearingAssessor's appraisers, (816) 858-3316Before June 30
Board of EqualizationForm from the County ClerkReturned before the second Monday in July; hearings in July
State Tax CommissionComplaint for Review of AssessmentSeptember 30, or thirty days after the board rules if that is later

Take photos, a recent sale of your property or an appraisal to the informal meeting. Increase notices are mailed by June 15. Paying under protest means paying the whole bill by December 31, writing "paid under protest" on the check and filing a written statement with the collector, as the State Tax Commission guide explains. Appeals on a rising value are worth the effort before a listing, since a buyer sees the assessed figure too.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Platte County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What relief programs apply in Platte County?

Two county-run credits go through the County Clerk, and neither freezes value. SB-190 is the senior tax credit, which protects a qualifying participant's base-year tax liability. SB-3, the Homestead Tax Credit enacted in April 2026, targets owner-occupied primary residences not already covered by SB-190 and limits yearly tax growth to 5 percent or the Consumer Price Index, whichever is greater. Its full effect should show in the 2027 cycle.

Homes in either program are still reassessed, and a Greater Than 15% notice does not remove a participant from the credit. Call the County Clerk at (816) 858-3340 about eligibility, and ask what paperwork to bring and when the application is due, since a missed window can mean waiting a full cycle. If you are selling a home that carries a credit, ask the clerk what happens to it after the sale and tell your closing agent what you learn. The state Property Tax Credit claim is separate and pays up to $1,100 to qualifying owner-occupants who are seniors or 100 percent disabled (Missouri Department of Revenue).

Selling with taxes owed

Get the latest bill, or look up the parcel on the assessor's Beacon search, before you list. Notices go to the owner of record at the last address the assessor has, so a seller who moved should file the assessor's change of address form so notices are not lost.

Ask the Collector in Platte City for payoff figures, and have the title company explain how the year is split at closing. Bring the latest statement, the parcel number and your current mailing address to that conversation, and tell the assessor if you have moved so notices follow you. Because the statement is due on receipt, a sale in November or December leaves little time between the bill arriving and the postmark deadline. A cash purchase can close fast, but the unpaid balance still comes out of your proceeds, so settle the figure before the closing date is set.

Frequently asked questions

When do Platte County property taxes become delinquent?

Late charges begin after December 31. The envelope must be postmarked by that date, and later payments are returned unless penalty and interest are included.

Where do I pay in person?

Go to the Collector's counter in the Administration Building at 415 3rd St., Room 212, Platte City, any weekday between 8 and 5. A 24-hour drop box sits outside the entrance to the government complex.

Did my value go up more than 15 percent?

Check the Assessor's Beacon search, which shows 2027 estimates beside the 2026 value. A projected increase over 15 percent, excluding new construction, triggers a mailed notice and an exterior inspection.

What is the deadline for a Board of Equalization appeal?

The County Clerk must receive the completed form ahead of the second Monday in July. The assessor also asks owners to meet an appraiser informally before June 30.

Does the SB-3 Homestead Tax Credit freeze my home value?

No. SB-3 limits tax growth on an eligible primary residence to 5 percent or the CPI, whichever is greater, and homes in the program are still reassessed. Ask the County Clerk at (816) 858-3340 about eligibility.
