Which office does what

Hillsboro's Administration Center, 729 Maple Street, houses all three offices you may need. One values each parcel (Assessor), one runs the first-level appeal board (County Clerk), and one sends out the bills and takes payment (Collector).

  • Assessor: 636-797-5343 for real estate, 636-797-5466 for personal property, office hours are 8 am to 5 pm, Monday to Friday.
  • County Clerk: 636-797-5478 for Board of Equalization appointments.
  • Collector: 636-797-5406, mailing address P.O. Box 100, Hillsboro, MO 63050.

None of these offices sets your rate. School, fire, ambulance and other districts do that for the land inside their boundaries, so two houses in different school districts, say Fox C-6 and Hillsboro R-3, can have quite different totals.

Housing in Jefferson County

Jefferson County is a Mississippi River county just south of St. Louis. Arnold has the most people, Hillsboro is where the courthouse sits, and the incorporated places also include Festus, De Soto, Crystal City, Herculaneum and Pevely. As of July 2025 there were 233,132 residents and 96,228 housing units. More than four in five homes are owner-occupied (82.2%), with a median value of $237,200.

Since so many households own, many tax bills are paid by mortgage servicers out of escrow. If that is you, the lender-request rule under due dates, below, matters.

How the Assessor values a home

The Assessor relies on mass appraisal. Building replacement cost less depreciation, plus land value, gives fair market value. Every parcel in Missouri is reassessed in odd-numbered years, which makes 2027 the coming cycle. The county then applies a percentage that depends on the property class.

Assessment levels used in Jefferson County
Property classShare of market value taxed
Residential19%
Commercial32%
Agricultural12%

A bill can move even without a reassessment. Adding a garage or an adjoining acre lifts assessed value, as does completing a house that was prorated during construction. A levy change approved by voters alters the total even if your value is unchanged.

Due dates and penalties

The tax is due by December 31 and delinquent from January 1. November brings the bills, first on the county website and then in the mail. Call the Collector if December 1 comes and goes with no bill, because the deadline still applies to you.

  • Pay at 729 Maple Street, online, or or by calling 1-877-289-0099. Cards, debit or credit, add a 2.5% convenience fee with a $1.95 minimum; an e-check adds $4.95.
  • For mail, the postmark must read December 31 or earlier. Ask your post office when its final pickup is.
  • A mortgage company has to send the Collector a written request for each bill it intends to pay. If a paper bill reached you, your lender never made that request.

The Collector cannot waive penalty or interest, a limit tied to section 139.100 and an Attorney General opinion. RSMo 140.100 adds an 18 percent penalty for each delinquent year on land in the back tax book, and land redeemed before the sale can be charged no more than 2 percent per month.

How to contest a value

Your first step is to phone the Assessor, whose appraiser will talk through the value and weigh anything you can show. A disagreement that survives that conversation goes to the Board of Equalization, and you file through the County Clerk. Each year the cutoff is the second Monday in July; in 2027 that is July 12.

  1. Ask the Assessor, 636-797-5343, for an informal review.
  2. Get forms and a hearing date from the County Clerk, 636-797-5478.
  3. Bring five copies of any written evidence: one per board member, one for the board secretary and one for the Assessor.
  4. A certified letter with the decision typically follows within 5 business days.
  5. Still unhappy? File a Complaint for Review of Assessment with the State Tax Commission and include the board's decision letter.

Commission filings are due September 30, or 30 days from the board's decision if that comes later, counted from the letter's date. An LLC, trust, corporation or estate must use an attorney to file.

The bill is still due December 31 while an appeal is pending. Paying under protest means full payment ahead of the delinquency date plus a written statement giving your grounds and your own figure for fair market value. The word protest scribbled on a check does nothing alone.

Tax relief for homeowners

Homeowners can look at two programs. Jefferson County has a Real Property Tax Credit for Seniors, enacted February 15, 2024, and the Assessor can explain it. The state also offers a Property Tax Credit Claim that gives back part of the real estate tax or rent paid over the year.

  • State credit maximums are $1,100 for owner-occupants and $750 for renters.
  • Eligibility: age 65 by December 31 of the prior year, 100% disability for you or your spouse, or age 60 or older with surviving spouse benefits.
  • Income limits, counting Social Security, are $30,000 for a single person and $34,000 for married homeowners.
  • File form MO-1040 with schedule MO-PTS, or form MO-PTC if you do not file an income tax return.

If a tornado, flood, fire or earthquake destroys your house, you can ask the Assessor to remove the residential value pro rata under section 137.082. Use the Destroyed Residential Property form.

Selling with taxes owed

At most closings the seller's share of the year's tax is credited on the settlement statement, and the buyer takes on the whole year's bill. Your settlement statement or title company shows the actual split.

A new deed recorded at the Recorder of Deeds office is what changes the owner in the Assessor's file. Names on real estate bills change only through a recorded deed, so a phone call alone will not update the owner or the mailing address.

  1. Ask the Collector for the amount due on every year, penalty and interest included, before you accept an offer.
  2. Give that figure to the title company so it can pay the balance from your proceeds.
  3. Confirm that your lender's escrow, if you have one, covers the current bill so it is not paid twice.

If your closing lands near the end of the year, ask the title company which bill it expects to pay and by what date, since the December 31 cutoff can fall between contract and closing. A cash sale follows the same path. The buyer's funds go through title, the delinquent years are paid first, and you keep what is left. Repairs and a lender's appraisal do not hold up the tax payoff.

Frequently asked questions

By what date must a Jefferson County real estate bill be paid?

December 31 of the tax year. A payment postmarked later is charged penalty and interest, and the Collector cannot waive either one.

When is the Jefferson County appeal deadline?

The Board of Equalization takes filings until the second Monday in July. Missouri reassesses in odd-numbered years, so the next notices arrive in 2027 with a July 12, 2027 filing date.

Who do I call if my Jefferson County tax bill never arrived?

Call the Collector at 636-797-5406. Owners should call if nothing shows up by December 1, and the December 31 deadline stays the same either way.

Does my mortgage lender pay the Jefferson County bill?

Only if it sent the Collector a written request for your bill. If the paper bill came to you, the lender did not ask for it, so ask the lender where it wants the bill sent.

Who pays the year's tax when I sell my Jefferson County house?

Usually the seller's portion is credited at closing and the buyer owes the whole year's bill. Your settlement statement lays out the split.

Who bills and who values

Two county offices share the job. The collector of revenue sends bills and takes payment, and the assessor puts a value on the land. The Franklin County Collector works from Room 103 at 400 E Locust in Union, phone 636-583-6353. Besides current and delinquent tax for the county and 64 other taxing entities, that desk handles levee, railroad and utility tax and merchant and manufacturer licenses.

Payment choices:

  • Online, through the Property Tax Bill Pay page on the county website
  • By phone, 877-690-3729, using jurisdiction code 3570
  • At the Collector's counter, by check or cash
  • By mail, to the address printed on the bill

Expect a small convenience fee on the online and phone options.

The assessor never calculates the tax, picks a rate or prints a bill. Every taxing jurisdiction picks its own levy, so a complaint about the rate belongs at that body's budget meeting.

Franklin County housing snapshot

Franklin County is a big exurban county south of the Missouri River in the St. Louis metro area, and Union is its seat. The population estimate is 108,090, a 3.3 percent gain on 2020. Housing units number 48,091, and owners live in 76.5 percent of occupied homes. A typical owner-occupied home is valued at $227,600. Builders pulled 794 permits in 2025.

Cities in the county are Berger, Gerald, New Haven, Pacific, St. Clair, Sullivan, Union and Washington. Inside any of them you owe the city as well, which means a Washington or Pacific address brings two sets of statements.

The assessment roll and your parcel record

More than 73,000 parcels sit on the roll: about 50,000 residential, 24,000 agricultural and 3,400 commercial. All real estate is reassessed on a two-year cycle, and the office mails over 20,000 notices of increased value in a year.

State law fixes the ratios. RSMo 137.115 puts houses at 19 percent of true value, with different percentages for farm and commercial ground. A residential increase above 15 percent that does not come from new building needs a site inspection before it stands.

Title companies and lenders call the assessor often, and the county's property search site lets you open your own parcel record first. Look at acreage, square footage and bedroom count there. A wrong entry can move the value.

Property tax calendar

The assessor's yearly calendar shows where your house sits in the cycle.

Utility and railroad reports reach the assessor by April 1, and the clerk certifies those values by April 20.

What the calendar means if you list in spring or fall

A house listed in spring is already carrying a value set on January 1, and the notice of any change reaches the owner of record. If you want to question it, the second Monday in July is your window, and nobody can file for you after it. A house listed in autumn is closer to a different problem: rates are certified on October 1, the bill is printed in November or December, and the money is due before the year ends. Ask the Collector whether the figure for your parcel is final before you agree to a closing date in that stretch.

Whenever you list, hold on to the latest bill and every assessor notice. Buyers' agents ask for them, and having them saves a trip to Union. If the property is a rental or has a personal property account, remember that the March 1 list deadline is separate from the real estate bill.

Contesting a valuation

Call the assessor's staff first. They sit down with owners informally, mostly in reassessment years, and aim to settle a concern before it becomes a Board filing. Ask which sales support the value, then compare them with houses on your block.

If that fails, file with the Board of Equalization by the July date in the calendar. Assessor staff lay out the facts to the Board. When a value rose 15 percent or more for a reason other than new building, RSMo 138.060 makes the assessor prove it.

The State Tax Commission comes next, with the county's attorney speaking for the assessor. A claim that the property is wholly exempt is a circuit court matter. Owners that are LLCs, trusts, estates or corporations must hire a lawyer to file.

Relief for seniors and disabled owners

No Missouri exemption removes a senior's or disabled owner's property from the tax roll. The state does run a credit for low-income seniors and disabled residents, paid as a refund or income tax credit and tied to property tax or rent paid. Read the rules on the Department of Revenue site, or call Aging Ahead at 636-629-3143.

If taxes go unpaid after December 31

A balance still open after December 31 is delinquent and picks up the 18 percent penalty in RSMo 140.100. For mailed checks, the postmark date decides.

You can contest a value and still pay: send the full amount, file a protest statement with the collector, and sue the collector within 90 days as RSMo 139.031 requires. The same section lets you apply within three years for a credit or refund of tax paid in error.

Parcels with old unpaid years are put up at the August tax sale. Paying the tax, penalty and costs any time before it takes the parcel off the list. The Collector's number for a parcel-specific payoff is 636-583-6353.

Taxes when you sell

Look up the parcel on the pay site and print what it shows. One call to 636-583-6353 will tell you if any earlier year is still open. The title company needs the parcel ID and a payoff number. How the current year splits between you and the buyer is written in the sales contract, so go over that clause together ahead of closing.

Inherited house, back taxes, tenants, repair debt? A cash offer lets the tax balance be paid from the price when you sign, and no lender appraisal or repair list slows things down. Deeds are filed with the Recorder of Deeds, and the county website's home page has a Record My Deeds link.

Frequently asked questions

How can I pay my Franklin County bill?

Walk in to Room 103 at 400 E Locust in Union, pay online, mail a check, or call 877-690-3729 and enter code 3570. Phone and online payments add a small fee.

When are Franklin County taxes due?

By December 31. After that they are delinquent and penalties start.

How do I contest a Franklin County assessment?

Speak with the assessor first. If that fails, the Board of Equalization takes filings until the second Monday in July, and the State Tax Commission follows.

How often does Franklin County reassess homes?

On a two-year cycle, with new construction added every year. Over 20,000 increase notices go out annually.

Can Franklin County seniors get tax relief?

The state offers a refund-style credit for income-limited seniors and disabled residents. The Homestead Preservation Act credit is not funded.

Offices that handle your tax bill

The Collector is staffed weekdays from half past eight until half past four and is shut on state and federal holidays. The Assessor's website offers real estate and personal property lookups by account number, name or address.

The county market

Stoddard County fills the southeast corner of Missouri. Bloomfield is the seat and Dexter the largest city. About 28,284 people live in 13,409 homes, and owners occupy 71.8% of them. The median owner-reported home value is $143,300, median rent is $760 and median household income is $57,957. Seven public districts reach into the county: Advance R-IV, Bell City R-II, Bernie R-XIII, Bloomfield R-XIV, Dexter R-XI, Puxico R-VIII and Richland R-I.

When payment is due

Collection opens November 1 and ends December 31. The County Clerk delivers the tax books in the fall, the bills are printed after that, and they reach mailboxes in November.

Once December 31 is behind you, added charges hit on the first of every month, in the amounts printed on the statement. A mailed check needs a U.S. Postal Service postmark dated within the month, since a payment that falls short of the added penalties is sent back. If the bill never reached you, the penalty still applies.

The Collector's website looks up a bill by owner name, parcel number, property address or account number, and shows payment history. You can pay with cash at the counter, a personal check, a money order or a cashier's check, or by card on the website or by phone, where a convenience fee applies. The drop box by the entrance to the government building is open around the clock, but a late check left there without the penalty comes back to you. Tax paid out of a mortgage escrow account will not appear in the online database.

Monthly installment plan

Yes, a plan exists for the real estate bill. The county has run it since the 2010 tax year. It starts from last year's real estate payment, divides it by eleven, and collects ten equal pieces, then the actual balance as the eleventh. Money leaves a checking or savings account automatically, on the 5th or the 20th.

  • You cannot join while any real estate tax is past due.
  • A parcel whose tax runs through a mortgage escrow is not eligible.
  • A missed withdrawal can end the plan, and any amount left unpaid at year end draws the usual penalties.

Homestead credit for older owners

A county resident who is 62 or older on January 1, owns the home and lives in it can lock in the real estate tax on that home. The credit does not exempt you from tax. You still pay a bill, just a frozen one.

First-time filers have from January 1 to June 30. Renewal paperwork is mailed beginning February 1 and is also due June 30. A notary must witness the first application, and the license or state ID has to show the home address. The homestead covers a primary residence on up to five acres, which leaves out barns, commercial ground and farmland.

New construction and additions are addressed too. Before you list, ask the Collector at (573) 568-3327 how a sale or a remodel would affect your frozen base year.

If your assessed value looks too high

Call the Assessor at (573) 568-3163 and ask for this year's Board of Equalization filing date. At the board, RSMo 138.060 removes any presumption that the assessor is right. In a county of this type the assessor must carry the burden of proof when a parcel's assessed value climbed 15% or more from the prior assessment, unless new construction or improvement explains the jump.

Paying while you contest follows RSMo 139.031. The whole bill is due before delinquency, along with a written statement of your grounds delivered to the Collector. A circuit court suit for recovery has to begin within 90 days of that protest.

Tax certificates and closing day

RSMo 140.150 allows land with unpaid tax to be offered for sale on the fourth Monday in August. Before that, the collector mails a letter to the record owner. When the assessed value is above $1,000, a second letter goes out by certified mail. Notices of delinquent tax certificate sales appear on the Collector's website.

At closing, the working rule is that taxes ride with the land, not the owner. The statement is passed to the buyer, and buyer and seller agree who pays what when the bill comes due. Buyers are expected to learn the tax status before they buy, so a title company will probably ask for a payoff or a proration. Missouri's Form MO-PTC is a separate state refund claim for some seniors, disabled owners and renters, and the Department of Revenue decides who qualifies.

Selling with a tax balance

Stoddard County is mostly rural, and its small offices are used to handling closings by phone and mail. A seller who lives out of town can order the payoff by phone, mail a check to P.O. Box 80 or pay by card on the website, so there is little reason to wait until the last week to deal with the bill. Keep the receipt or a printout of your payment history for the closing file.

Here is the order that usually works for a Stoddard County seller. First, look up your bill on the Collector's website by owner name, parcel number or address, and confirm what is owed. Second, call (573) 568-3327 if anything looks wrong or if you are on the installment plan. Third, give the title company the payoff or proration figure so it can appear on the settlement statement. Fourth, check whether a senior homestead credit is in place, because the buyer will want to know how it affects the first bill after the sale.

If you owe tax when you decide to sell, call the Collector first for a payoff figure and make sure the installment plan, if you use one, is settled or current. Any unpaid balance comes out of your proceeds at the table. A cash buyer can close without waiting for a lender, which helps when you want the tax cleared before the August sale list, but compare the offer with what a listing would leave after fees and repairs.

Frequently asked questions

Where is Stoddard County property tax paid?

At the Collector of Revenue, 401 S. Prairie St in Bloomfield, by mail to P.O. Box 80, Bloomfield, MO 63825, or online through the Collector's website.

What is the last day to pay without penalty?

December 31. Collection begins November 1, and extra charges start accruing on the first of each month after the deadline.

Is there a way to spread the bill over the year?

Yes, for real estate tax only. Ten equal monthly withdrawals are followed by a final payment of the balance. Past-due accounts and escrowed parcels cannot join.

Which party pays the tax at a sale?

Buyer and seller decide that at closing. The statement should go to the buyer, and taxes stay with the property.

What age qualifies for the homestead freeze?

Sixty-two on January 1, plus ownership and primary residence of the home. New applications are accepted from January 1 through June 30.

Howell County offices and hours

Collector and assessor both work from the county building on the West Plains square, 35 Court Square. The County Collector is in Room 201, phone (417) 256-4001, fax (417) 257-0090. The counter is open Monday through Friday from 8:30 am until 4:30 pm, noon hour included, and shuts for state holidays.

The assessor is in Suite 202 at (417) 256-8284 and opens at 8:00 am. The assessor's site offers GIS mapping and a subscription parcel search at howell.missouriassessors.com. The collector does more than houses: it prepares separate statements for personal property such as cars, trucks and boats, for real estate, and for utilities such as railroads and gas lines, and it issues merchant licenses.

Paying your Howell County tax bill

Mailing starts in November, and each statement is due when it arrives. Delinquency begins after December 31, and a check postmarked January 1 or later is returned unless late fees are included. A statement that never turns up still leaves the tax owing, so phone the office if one has not come by the end of November.

Ways to pay Howell County property tax
MethodHow it works

Phone1-800-652-0405, current taxes only; enter county number 18 and the PIN from your statement
MailPostmarked no later than December 31

Each month the collector passes what it has taken in to the taxing entities that levy against your parcel.

Who owes the tax if you sell or move mid-year

Under RSMo 137.075, liability attaches to whoever holds property on January 1, even a buyer who closes that same day. A person who moves out of Missouri in June still owes tax for that whole year. The law gives no proration.

That rule is written mostly around vehicles and other personal property, which owners list with the assessor before March 1. A house works differently in practice. What you and the buyer each pay of the year's real estate bill comes from the sale contract and settlement statement, so read the proration clause first.

What share of a home's value is taxed

Homes are taxed on 19 percent of true value, farmland on 12 and commercial property on 32, as set in RSMo 137.115. Values are reset every odd year.

  • Any raise over 15 percent on a home, unless new building caused it, calls for an on-site inspection.
  • You may ask the inspector to come inside, and the notice must give you thirty days to do so.
  • On appeal, RSMo 138.060 makes the assessor prove a raise of that size is justified.

Open your parcel record on the assessor's site before you call so you can quote the parcel number. The subscription search there also shows what nearby properties are carried at, which is useful when you want to compare your value with a neighbor's.

Your options if the number looks wrong

Begin with the Board of Equalization, which takes filings until the second Monday in July. The State Tax Commission is the next level and allows 30 days from the date of the Board's letter. A stipulation signed with the assessor ends the case permanently.

Paying under protest is a separate tool. RSMo 139.031 asks for the whole bill before delinquency, a written explanation filed with the collector and a lawsuit against the collector within ninety days. The collector holds the contested share in its own fund while the case runs. A tax paid by mistake can be credited or refunded if the taxpayer applies within three years.

The August delinquent tax sale

The collector holds the sale on the fourth Monday in August, and RSMo 140.150 agrees. Until the gavel falls, an owner can settle by paying the tax, penalty, interest and costs. The collector mails notice to the record owner, though a letter that goes astray does not wipe out the debt.

If you owe a balance, ask (417) 256-4001 for a payoff so the title company can pay it out of your proceeds.

Howell County housing at a glance

Along the Arkansas line, Howell County is led by West Plains. It has an estimated 40,798 people and 18,288 housing units, and 70.3 percent of homes are lived in by owners. Expect a median owned-home value of $173,000 and median rent of $733. Owner costs average $1,109 with a mortgage and $394 without. With only 67 permits issued in 2025, buyers mostly choose from existing houses.

Other towns include Brandsville, Mountain View and Willow Springs.

Three kinds of statement

The collector issues separate statements for personal property, real estate and utilities, and a homeowner usually sees two of them. The real estate statement covers the house and land. The personal property statement covers vehicles, boats and similar items that you listed with the assessor before March 1, so a seller who owns a truck or boat should expect a second envelope.

Each kind can be delinquent on its own. When you ask for a payoff, say clearly that you want every statement tied to your name, then ask whether the amount includes late fees. The phone line at 1-800-652-0405 handles current taxes only, so an older balance has to be paid at the counter or by another route.

A practical checklist for the week before closing

  1. Confirm with Room 201 that the real estate statement for the year is paid or that the payoff is known.
  2. Ask whether any personal property statement is open under your name.
  3. Print the parcel record from the assessor's site and compare it with the deed.
  4. Give the title company the payoff, the parcel number and the contract's proration clause.
  5. Keep the receipt and put it with the settlement statement.

A drop box outside the county building takes payments after hours, and a check in the mail must carry a postmark no later than December 31 to count as timely.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Selling a Howell County house with taxes due

Start with a statement from Room 201 and a call to (417) 256-4001 to see whether an earlier year is open. Ask for a payoff figure and give it to the title company, along with the parcel number from the assessor's site. Keep the receipt with your closing papers.

Remember that the year's bill is assigned by your contract, not by the county. If a lien, a tenant or a repair list is slowing a normal sale, a cash buyer can close without a lender's appraisal and the title company pays the county balance from your proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

What phone number pays a Howell County tax bill?

Call 1-800-652-0405 for current taxes. Enter county number 18, then the PIN printed on your statement. Back taxes cannot be paid on that line.

Who is the Howell County assessor's office?

It is in Suite 202 at 35 Court Square, West Plains, open weekdays from 8:00 am to 4:30 pm. The phone is (417) 256-8284.

When must personal property be listed in Howell County?

Before March 1 each year. Property is assessed as it stood on January 1.

Is tax prorated if I leave Missouri?

No, the tax rests on what you held on January 1, and the law has no proration. A home sale contract can still split that year's real estate bill between buyer and seller.

Where can I check my parcel before an appeal?

Use the assessor's site, howell.missouriassessors.com, or call (417) 256-8284. Have the parcel number ready, and file any Board of Equalization appeal by the second Monday in July.

Who handles property tax in Phelps County?

Two offices in the courthouse at 200 N Main Street, Rolla, MO 65401 divide the work. One values the property and the other bills it and takes the money. Neither sets a rate. Voters in each taxing district do that.

  • Assessor: Suite 126, (573) 458-6135, fax (573) 458-6149, weekdays 8:00 to 4:30
  • Collector: Suite 129, (573) 458-6155, collectorgroup@phelpscounty.org, open weekdays through lunch until 4:30
  • County Clerk: (573) 458-6115, for levy and tax rate questions
  • Recorder of Deeds: (573) 458-6095, for the deed itself

The assessor cannot discuss the dollar amount of a bill. That office answers questions about assessed and market value, and the collector handles the rest.

How the bill is calculated

The collector offers two formulas. Divide the assessed value by the adjustment factor to estimate the assessor's market value, then divide the assessed value by 100 and multiply by the levy to get the tax. The assessment rates are 19 percent of market value for residential land, 12 for farmland and 32 for commercial use, as RSMo 137.115 provides.

That assessed figure, counted in hundreds, is multiplied by the combined levy of the school, fire, city and other districts covering your parcel. You pay only the districts that apply to your address, not every levy in the county.

Real estate is valued on a two year cycle, but the 2025 reassessment was larger than usual. The state tax commission found that local values had slipped out of the 90 to 110 percent compliance band after several years of rising sales prices. Average residential assessed value rose by about 10 percent that year, while agricultural and commercial values stayed flat apart from new construction or changes in condition.

If the assessor visits your property

Field staff are canvassing the county to refresh photos of homes and outbuildings and to note condition, concentrating on parcels not visited in more than five years. The work is required by RSMo 137.130. Staff drive white Ford Bronco Sports with the assessor's logo on the doors, wear vests marked Phelps County Assessor and carry a county photo ID. Owners who asked to be called first are called when possible.

State law also limits large jumps. Under RSMo 137.115, a residential parcel cannot rise more than 15 percent without a physical inspection unless new construction explains it, and the owner has at least thirty days after written notice to ask for an interior inspection.

How to appeal your valuation

Begin by calling or visiting the assessor at (573) 458-6135 and asking which comparable sales and condition notes support your number. Missouri law favors an owner who disagrees. An increase must be reported to the record owner, who gets a hearing if the county's equalization board reviews it (RSMo 137.180).

Ask the county clerk at (573) 458-6115 for the board's forms and filing deadline. The board begins with no assumption that the assessor is right, and an increase of 15 percent or more outside new construction leaves the burden of proof on the assessor (RSMo 138.060). The next stop is the State Tax Commission, open by the statutory date or thirty days after the board finishes, whichever is later (RSMo 138.430).

Due dates and payment options

Statements go out in early November. December 31 is the last day, and a postmark after it brings late fees. Send mail with the stub, called the statement topper, because it carries the account number. Bank bill pay services often send errors and no topper, so the collector advises against them.

Ways to pay at the Phelps County Collector

The collector keeps none of the online fees. One check can cover any mix of real estate and personal property statements, but the amount must be exact, because a payment written for the wrong sum cannot be processed. Installment plans exist for real estate and personal property, so ask at the counter for the form. If no bill has arrived by Thanksgiving, call right away.

Senior tax freeze

Phelps County seniors may qualify for a freeze on real estate taxes under Senate Bill 190 as expanded by Senate Bill 756. The applicant must be at least 62 by December 31 of the application year, own and live in the home as a primary residence, and be responsible for its taxes. Only one owner needs to be 62.

Applications are taken from March 1 through May 31. The freeze starts with the 2027 tax year, and the collector asks for at least 90 days to process. After that, participants send an affidavit every year during the same March through May window.

  • The freeze covers one primary residence only and is not retroactive to age 62.
  • It does not carry over to a new home; a move means a new application and a new base year.
  • A transfer of title removes the home from the program, as does a missed annual affidavit.
  • Debt levies and newly voted tax increases still show on the bill.

Questions go to the collector at (573) 458-6155 or seniortaxrelief@phelpscounty.org.

Unpaid taxes and the August auction

Delinquent parcels are auctioned once a year on the fourth Monday in August, starting at 10:00 am in the Community Room of the courthouse, under RSMo 140.150. Notice runs in the Rolla Daily News on three consecutive Wednesdays beforehand, and the list appears on the collector's website.

A buyer does not own the house right away. The owner, a lienholder or an occupant can redeem during the year after the sale by paying the collector the purchase amount and costs, and the buyer earns simple interest of 10 percent a year on the tax and cost portion. The county advertises many more parcels than it sells, because most owners pay before the day arrives. If you are behind, ask the collector what it takes to come off the list before the sale.

For a seller, this matters at the listing stage. Clear any delinquent year before you go under contract, since a title company will want it paid at closing. A cash buyer can still close quickly, though the back tax comes out of your proceeds.

Phelps County at a glance

Phelps County is in central Missouri, and Rolla is both the seat and the largest city, home to Missouri University of Science and Technology. Other communities include St. James, Newburg, Doolittle and Edgar Springs. The July 2025 estimate is 45,247 residents and 20,625 housing units, and 61.7 percent of households own their home. A typical home is valued at $206,500, median gross rent is $798 and median household income is $58,396. School districts include Rolla 31, St. James R-I, Newburg R-II and Phelps County R-III.

Frequently asked questions

When must Phelps County real estate tax be paid?

December 31. Bills are mailed in early November, and a payment not postmarked by December 31 incurs late fees.

Who decides my tax rate?

Not the assessor, who sets value only. Each taxing district sets its levy by a vote of its residents, and the county clerk at (573) 458-6115 can answer rate questions.

Who gets the tax bill if I bought my house mid-year?

The new owner pays the bill when it comes due. The buyer receives a credit at closing for the tax the seller owed for the year, and bills show the previous owner's name if the sale came after September 1.

When can I apply for the senior tax freeze?

Applications are accepted from March 1 through May 31. Call the collector at (573) 458-6155 to confirm the current year's window.

What day is the delinquent tax auction?

The fourth Monday in August at 10:00 am, in the courthouse Community Room in Rolla.

Christian County housing snapshot

Christian County sits in the Ozarks between Springfield and Branson. Ozark holds the courthouse and Nixa has the most residents. The county keeps adding people, from 88,842 at the 2020 census to an estimated 96,725 in mid-2025. About three homes in four (75.9%) are lived in by their owners, so a listing here usually competes with other owner-occupied houses and with new builds.

  • The county had 38,594 housing units in 2025 and builders pulled 495 permits that year.
  • The 2020 to 2024 middle value for an owner-occupied home was $274,900.
  • Median household income is $83,437.

Two offices matter for tax, and both work out of the historic courthouse on the Ozark square. The Assessor decides value. The Collector of Revenue sends the statements.

Collector and Assessor contacts

  • Collector of Revenue: 100 W. Church, Room 101, Ozark, MO 65721, (417) 582-4330. Weekday hours are 8:00 to 4:30, and the counter stays open at lunch.
  • Assessor: real estate questions at 417-582-4310, personal property at 417-582-4320.
  • Payment options include the counter, the mail, christiancountycollector.com, the toll-free number printed on the bill, and a drop box on the west side of the courthouse that is available around the clock.

The Collector collects what the Assessor's records say and has no power to change a statement. If the mailing address, vehicle list or legal description is wrong, fix it with the Assessor first. The office refuses partial payments and wrong amounts.

2026 due date

The 2026 statements went into the mail in early November. You can pay the day one arrives, and the balance turns delinquent after December 31. Mail must be postmarked 12/31/26 by the USPS, and the website stops taking payments at 11:59 p.m. that evening. A glitch on the phone line or website buys no extra time, the Collector says. If you escrow through a lender, confirm the lender has paid before the end of the year.

Owners in four small towns can pay close to home. Collector staff set up from 9 a.m. to noon on specific days at the city halls in Billings, Clever, Sparta and Highlandville. Only cash, check or money order is taken there (no cards), with checks in blue or black ink. Carry the full statement, and call the office for the posted days.

No statement by the end of November means a phone call to the Collector. Mail that goes missing does not cancel the tax.

Fees for paying electronically

A processing charge is added on top of the tax for electronic payments. None of it goes to the county, and RSMo 139.055 lets the cost land only on those who pick the electronic route.

Way to payFee

How the Assessor values property

The Assessor prices every taxable item in the county using its January 1 condition. Its roll holds more than 42,951 real estate parcels and over 38,457 personal property accounts, and total assessed value for 2025 tops $2 billion. State class rates turn market value into assessed value: residential 19 percent, commercial 32 percent, agricultural land 12 percent.

Value covers only part of the math. Each taxing district also sets a levy, and the Assessor tallies thirteen school districts, eight road districts, ten cities, nine fire districts and nine other districts for services like ambulance, senior programs and the junior college. Which of them overlap your parcel determines the total, so read the district names on your bill. The Assessor's page also hosts Value Change Notices, exemption applications and address change forms.

How to contest an assessment

An owner who objects to a value can climb from the Assessor to a county board and finally the State Tax Commission. Under RSMo 137.275, the Board of Equalization must receive your appeal by the second Monday in July. If the board's answer is unsatisfactory, RSMo 138.430 allows a commission appeal within the chapter 138 deadline, or 30 days after the board's last action if that is later.

  • Study your Value Change Notice and compare it with the market data the Assessor posts.
  • Phone 417-582-4310 and request an informal review of the number.
  • Get the board's form and hearing dates from the County Clerk.
  • When assessed value climbed 15 percent or more, RSMo 138.060 the Assessor must carry the burden of proof, except where new construction caused the increase.

Senior tax credit

Strict rules govern the Senate Bill 190 senior citizen real estate tax credit, and both the county home page and the Assessor's page post them. An approved owner renews with no new paperwork as long as they still qualify and added no improvements. A spouse who has just reached the age must file an application.

  • First-time forms are available March 1, 2027, and the Collector's office in Room 101 takes them through June 15, 2027.
  • Applicants need to be 62 or older by midnight on December 31, 2026.
  • The house must lie in Christian County and have been the applicant's primary residence since at least June 29, 2026.
  • Pay the 2026 taxes, finish the personal property assessment and have each applicant's signature notarized.

Selling with a tax bill due

Whoever owns the property owes all the tax on it, and the obligation is fixed as of January 1. Your title company can explain how the closing statement splits the year. Ask the Collector for the exact balance ahead of closing day.

Here is a workable order of operations. First, find your newest statement and jot down the parcel number and taxing districts. Second, get a written payoff figure from the Collector. Third, let the title company pay whatever is owed from your proceeds. Fourth, once the deed records, send the Collector and Assessor the buyer's name and mailing address so the next bill goes out correctly. Cash Home Buyers can close without a lender in the middle, which helps when a house carries back taxes or needs work, and the closing agent still settles the tax line.

Frequently asked questions

By what date must 2026 Christian County taxes be paid?

Pay by December 31, 2026. Mail must be postmarked 12/31/26 and the website closes at 11:59 p.m. that night. After that the balance is delinquent, and problems with the phone or web system do not move the date.

Where do I pay in person?

Go to Room 101 at 100 W. Church in Ozark on a weekday between 8:00 and 4:30. The courthouse's west side has a drop box that never closes, and Billings, Clever, Sparta and Highlandville host city hall payment days.

What are the card fees on a tax payment?

A credit card costs 2.45 percent of the balance extra, a debit card $4.00 and an e-check $2.00. The county keeps none of it. Paying in person by cash, check or money order has no fee.

Who sets the value of my home?

The Assessor does, using the January 1 condition and the state class rates of 19, 32 and 12 percent for residential, commercial and agricultural land. Real estate questions go to 417-582-4310. Each tax district then applies its own levy.

Can seniors reduce their tax bill?

Maybe, if you qualify for the SB 190 senior citizen real estate tax credit. New applications run March 1 to June 15, 2027, for owners who are 62 by December 31, 2026. Those already approved renew on their own.

Cass County market snapshot

Pressed against the Kansas border, Cass County is part of greater Kansas City, with Harrisonville as its courthouse town. The county has grown to 115,859 people (July 2025), a 7.5% gain on 2020, and 75.6% of its homes have owners living in them. New subdivisions in Belton, Raymore and Peculiar sit near resale houses, which gives an older home in Harrisonville or Pleasant Hill real competition when pricing.

Twelve school districts touch Cass, including Harrisonville R-IX, Belton, Raymore-Peculiar R-II, Pleasant Hill R-III, Archie R-V and Lee's Summit R-VII. Schools, fire protection and the library each levy separately. Equal assessed values therefore don't guarantee equal bills, and the district names on your statement show why.

Collector and Assessor offices

The two offices sit side by side on Cantrell Road in Harrisonville.

  • Collector: 2725 Cantrell Road, 816-380-8377, collector@casscounty.com. Counter service runs Monday to Friday, eight to four-thirty.
  • Assessor: 2733 Cantrell Road, 816-380-8400.
  • County Clerk: Historic Courthouse, 102 E. Wall Street. The Clerk handles the paperwork for the Board of Equalization.

A drop box for the Collector is at Annex 1, 201 W. Wall Street, and anything placed in it before midnight on December 31 counts as on time. Property tax is not paid at the Treasurer's office, and deeds are filed with the Recorder of Deeds. Search records or print a receipt through casscountycollector.org.

Due date and late penalties

Once your real estate statement arrives, you may pay it, and the hard stop is December 31. The county mails statements during November. A mailed check is judged by its U.S. Postal Service postmark, and metered postage from a private machine is refused. No statement by the end of November? Phone 816-380-8377.

Starting January 1 the Collector adds penalties and fees, which may reach 25 percent in the first delinquent year. A bill that never showed up doesn't excuse the debt. Tax is a claim on the land itself, so the next owner inherits any unpaid amount.

Statements carry whatever owner and address are on file when they print. A sale closing in October or later can therefore produce a bill in the old owner's name. If that is you, hand the Collector the buyer's name and mailing address. A buyer with nothing in hand by December 10 should call.

How the tax bill is figured

The bill comes from two things: the Assessor's value, and the levy from every taxing body covering the parcel. Divide assessed value by 100, then multiply by the combined rate.

  • Homes and other residential property: 19 percent of market value
  • Commercial property: 32 percent
  • Farm ground: 12 percent

Every odd-numbered year the county updates values across the board, while new construction is added when finished. If levies fall, a higher value may still leave your bill unchanged, and levies are normally set in September. Whether Cass offers the homestead credit in RSMo 137.1050 is a question for the Assessor at 816-380-8400, so ask before assuming it applies to the home you're selling.

How to appeal a Cass County value

Only market value is up for debate. Complaining that the bill is too high won't move the Board. What does help: photographs of defects, what your property sold for recently, or an appraiser's testimony.

  1. Start by discussing the value with the Assessor's staff.
  2. Mail or deliver the Board of Equalization appeal form to the Assessor with a July postmark by the posted date.
  3. If the Board does not satisfy you, the State Tax Commission is next: file by September 30, or 30 days after the Board's last action when that is later.

The County Commission appoints Board members and the County Clerk's office processes the filings. Look for the next appeal season after the 2027 reassessment. The statutes behind this are RSMo 138.430 and RSMo 137.275.

Tax certificate sale in August

Tax certificates are auctioned in the Harrisonville courthouse, 102 E. Wall Street, starting at 10 a.m. on August's fourth Monday. Expect the next one in August 2027. Land becomes eligible when its real estate tax is still unpaid after March 1 of the year after it was billed. RSMo 140.150 fixes the sale day and has the Collector notify the record owner before the list is published.

Owners may settle the back tax, penalty, interest and costs before the auction, and the Collector's website has a section for bidders. For a seller, a listing is a deadline. Paying the balance at closing removes the parcel.

Selling with taxes owed

Behind on tax and ready to sell? Ask the Collector for the precise balance with penalty and interest, then pass it to the title company so it appears on the settlement statement. Once paid, the parcel falls off any certificate sale list.

Gather three things before you list: the parcel number from your latest statement, the Collector's payoff figure, and the name of your lender if it escrows. With those in hand the title company can order the payoff letters without delay and your closing date won't hinge on a tax question.

Afterward, give the Collector the new owner's name and mailing address so November's statement goes to the right mailbox. A bill that still reaches you for a sold house should be forwarded along with those details, not paid out of your own pocket.

Property tax at closing

Closing usually splits the year's tax, with the buyer credited for each month or day you owned the home. The Collector receives nothing at the table. The buyer later pays the whole annual bill by December 31. A lender that escrows your tax should hear about the payoff, since it normally refunds the cushion or applies it to the loan.

The Recorder's FAQ promises same-day to 24-hour turnaround on real estate recordings, skipping weekends and holidays. Recorded deeds show no sale price. Staff there won't phone out closing details or search for liens, so lean on the title company, because liens can also sit with the courts or the Collector.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay Cass County property tax?

Bring it to the Collector at 2725 Cantrell Road in Harrisonville, weekdays. The drop box at 201 W. Wall Street counts until midnight on December 31, and casscountycollector.org lets you view bills online.

What does a late payment cost?

Penalties and fees can climb to 25 percent during the first year of delinquency, starting after December 31. By mail, only a U.S. postmark of December 31 or earlier keeps you on time.

Who covers the tax at closing, the buyer or the seller?

The year's tax is generally split, with the buyer credited for the stretch the seller owned the house. The Collector gets no money at closing, and the buyer pays the entire bill by December 31.

When does the county auction tax certificates?

Every August on the fourth Monday, 10 a.m., at the courthouse, 102 E. Wall Street, Harrisonville. Land can be offered if its real estate tax is still open after March 1 of the next year.

What is the first step to dispute my value?

Phone the Assessor at 816-380-8400. If that fails, send the Board of Equalization form to the same office with a July postmark by the deadline, and take any remaining dispute to the State Tax Commission.

Lincoln County housing snapshot

Eastern Missouri's Lincoln County faces Illinois across the Mississippi and belongs to the St. Louis area, with Troy as its seat. It is a fast-growing place: 52,566 residents in 2010, 59,574 in 2020 and 66,676 by July 2025, an 11.9% gain over the 2020 base. Housing units numbered 24,289, and builders pulled 252 permits during 2025.

Owners hold 79.0% of households. The median owner-occupied home is about $244,300, typical gross rent is $961, and 92.3% of residents were in the same house a year earlier, so turnover is low. Five public school districts cover the county; whichever one serves you puts its levy on the bill.

Who sets and who bills the tax

Go to 3 Front Street in Troy for the Assessor and to 1 Front Street for the Collector of Revenue, whose number is 636-528-0316. An online taxpayer portal looks up records by name, statement number or parcel number.

Think of a bill in three pieces. Value comes from the Assessor. The rate is chosen by the school, city or fire district from its own budget, and the Assessor plays no part in it. The Collector gathers what is owed.

The money is split among the state, county, ambulance, hospital, SB-40 board, county health center, schools, cities and fire districts. This office also collects drainage and neighborhood improvement district charges and merchant license fees, and takes escrow payments from mortgage holders.

How homes are assessed

For tax purposes a house counts for 19% of its market value, farmland for 12% and commercial property for 32%. Odd-numbered years (2021, 2023, 2025) are revaluation years, measured as of January 1. In the even years in between, the Assessor looks only for new or lost improvements.

Appraisers visit each parcel every year, driving marked county vehicles and wearing ID badges. Call the office if a person without identification is on your land. During a revaluation the staff set recent sale prices beside their own appraisals to decide whether land and buildings rise.

A raised value arrives with a Notice of Change in Value. You can request an informal hearing and then take the dispute to the Board of Equalization. Filing closes the second Monday of July, the board meets on the third Monday, and the State Tax Commission comes after it.

What happens at the tax sale?

Three delinquent years puts real estate on the sale list. The sale itself is on the courthouse east steps, fourth Monday in August, 10 a.m. An owner can still pay everything beforehand, and the Collector reports that plenty do once the ad is published.

Registration opens at 8 a.m. in Room 103 of the courthouse. Each bidder signs an affidavit swearing no delinquent tax is owed and has to show up personally. Out-of-state bidders name a Lincoln County citizen as their agent. Bidding opens at the taxes, interest and charges.

A winning bidder holds a certificate of purchase and pays taxes that come due later, yet has no right to possess the property while the one-year redemption period runs. The county treasurer keeps any amount bid above the opening figure for the owner of record, and after three unclaimed years it goes to the schools. Would-be buyers are told to consult an attorney first.

Paying or protesting a bill

Look up your bill on the taxpayer portal, call the office, or go to 1 Front Street in Troy. Searches take a statement number (R followed by digits for real estate), a parcel number or an owner name, and the portal returns up to 100 records.

A value protest works like this: send the complete bill to the Collector by December 31, label it a protest, and enclose your reasons and the value you claim. Postmarks of December 31 or earlier count for mailed payments.

Attorneys are required for LLCs, trusts, estates and corporations. Someone who got no notice of an increase, or who bought within 30 days after the statements were mailed, can go directly to the State Tax Commission.

From statement to closing

A typical sequence for a seller with an open balance looks like this.

  1. Search the taxpayer portal with your parcel number or name and note every statement that shows a balance.
  2. Phone 636-528-0316 and ask for a written payoff covering each open year, with penalty and interest.
  3. Send the payoff to your title company and say which year is the current one.
  4. Check the Assessor's record for owner name and acreage, and correct anything wrong before the contract is signed.
  5. At closing, confirm that the settlement statement shows the Collector being paid from your side.

Doing this before listing means the buyer's title search turns up no surprises and no tax sale list entry. Keep the paid receipt and the payoff letter together in your closing file, since either one answers a lender's or a buyer's question about the tax history in a single glance, which keeps the final days before closing calm.

Selling with taxes owed

Pull up your parcel record first, and get a written payoff from the Collector. Make sure the Assessor lists the correct owner and acreage. Find out whether drainage, neighborhood improvement or other district charges are on your bill.

  • Match the statement against the title company's closing statement.
  • Ask whether any year is on the August tax sale list.
  • If the owner is an older homeowner, ask the Collector about senior relief programs.
  • If the sale closes after August 31, ask the Collector who will receive the statement.

Closing takes the payoff out of the sale price, which is why the number should be on paper before you sign.

The steps are identical for a cash sale. A buyer who is not waiting on a loan can usually close fast enough to clear a delinquent year before the August list is published, and you walk away without the sale or a bidder's lien on the property.

Frequently asked questions

Is Lincoln County property tax due December 31?

Yes. A mailed payment needs a postmark on or before that date to avoid penalty and interest.

On what date is the Lincoln County tax sale?

The fourth Monday in August, at 10 a.m. on the courthouse east steps in Troy. Bidder registration starts at 8 a.m. in Room 103.

How often is Lincoln County real estate revalued?

Every two years, in odd-numbered years such as 2025 and 2027, as of January 1. The even years pick up new construction and lost improvements.

When must I file with the Lincoln County Board of Equalization?

By the second Monday in July. The board convenes on the third Monday in July.

Which Lincoln County office do I call about a balance?

Call the Collector of Revenue at 636-528-0316. For a question about value, contact the Assessor at 3 Front Street in Troy.

Which Warren County offices handle a property tax bill?

Property tax in Warren County runs through two suites of the Administration Building on Mockingbird Lane in Warrenton. Julie Schaumberg is the Collector, in Suite 200, at 636-456-3330, and her staff mails the bills and receives payment.

The Collector keeps weekday hours from eight until four-thirty, and email goes to collector@warrencountymo.gov. It states that it cannot add to or change a tax statement unless the Assessor makes the change first. Questions about value belong with the Assessor, and questions about paying belong with the Collector.

The Collector's site posts a 2026 rate PDF, a side by side of 2025 and 2026 rates, a tax sale list and a holiday calendar. The Assessor's site offers parcel and personal property searches, and it says emailed assessment forms are not accepted. Use the e-file option or the mail.

When are Warren County property taxes due?

The Collector mails statements in the first week of November, and December 31 is the last safe day. No bill by Thanksgiving? Phone the Collector. An unreceived statement still leaves the tax, and any late charge, owed.

With the Thanksgiving and Christmas closures, the number of open days before the deadline is smaller than it looks. A 24 hour drop box stands to the right of the entrance.

How does the Assessor value a house in Warren County?

Real estate here is revalued every second year, in the odd-numbered ones, on January 1 values. That puts the most recent cycle in 2025 and the coming one in 2027. In even years the only changes come from new construction or demolition.

Field appraisers visit every parcel, measure any added square footage and adjust depreciation on buildings. State law fixes the taxed share of value: 19 percent for residences, 12 percent for farm ground and 32 percent for commercial property. A jump of more than 15 percent on a home, apart from new building, requires a physical inspection first.

Rates come from elsewhere. Schools, the county, fire districts and other taxing bodies vote on theirs, and your total depends on which of them cover your address.

How do you appeal a Warren County assessment?

The Notice of Change in value arrives when reassessment or new construction raises a figure. Weigh it against what a buyer would pay.

  • Still no change? Book a Board of Equalization hearing through the Assessor before the legal cutoff.
  • The Board's ruling can go to the State Tax Commission, which hears appeals filed within 30 days of that ruling or by the chapter's own date if later.

The Assessor's page says a complaint that taxes are high is not relevant testimony. Only the market value of the house counts. An owner who pays the whole current bill before it goes delinquent can lodge a written protest with the Collector, then has 90 days to file suit in circuit court. With a timely Commission appeal pending, the disputed slice is held in a separate fund.

What happens if tax is still owed when a Warren County house sells?

The Assessor's site says whoever owns property on January 1 is liable for that calendar year's tax. A March closing therefore leaves the seller as the named owner for the year, so the settlement sheet needs to say who covers the bill.

Get the parcel's balance from the Collector ahead of closing day. The counter refuses short or wrong amounts, and any delinquent year has to be settled before the current one. Confirm the oldest year first, because anything delinquent comes ahead of the current bill.

Does a move out of Warren County change the vehicle tax bill?

No. Vehicles are taxed on what the owner held on January 1, according to the Assessor's site, even if the car was sold the next day or the owner left Missouri in June. The law has no proration.

A seller moving soon after closing still gets that year's personal property statement, with the same December 31 postmark date. The Assessor adds that a taxpayer arriving in Missouri on March 1, 2026 is first assessed on January 1, 2027, and pays that bill in December 2027.

Owners with a mortgage paid a median $1,485 a month and those without paid $499. Builders took out 360 permits in 2025, against 212 in Stone and 226 in Webster. Work is common: 62.8 percent of adults are in the civilian labor force, and the county's transportation and warehousing receipts came to $113.4 million in 2022.

Where is Warren County and which schools serve it?

Warren County lies on the north side of the Missouri River and is part of the St. Louis metropolitan area. It covers 438 square miles and was established on January 5, 1833. Interstate 70, U.S. Route 40, Route 47 and Route 94 cross it, and Route 94 is known as the Missouri Weinstrasse for its vineyards.

Warrenton is the county seat. The other cities are Foristell, Marthasville, Truesdale and Wright City, and the villages are Innsbrook, Pendleton and Three Creeks. Public school districts are Warren County R-III in Warrenton and Wright City R-II. The statement shows which district a house sits in, and that choice moves the rate.

Neighbors are Lincoln County to the north, St. Charles County to the east, Franklin County to the south, Gasconade County to the southwest and Montgomery County to the west. The county belongs to the Missouri Rhineland, with award-winning wineries on both sides of the river. At the Collector's office, 101 Mockingbird Lane, Suite 200, Warrenton. You can also pay online, by mail, through the vendor phone line or in the 24 hour drop box. The office number is 636-456-3330.

What is the Warren County property tax deadline?

Mail it with a December 31 postmark. Bills go out the first week of November, and earlier delinquent years are cleared before the current one.

In 2027. Values reset in odd-numbered years, and in 2026 only new construction or demolition changes a parcel's figure.

Can I make a partial payment on a Warren County bill?

No. The Collector says it cannot take incorrect or partial payments. One check can still cover several bills.

Ask the Assessor for an informal hearing first, then a Board of Equalization appointment. Bring a sale price or appraisal, because the size of the tax bill is not evidence.

When a parcel's assessed valuation jumped by 15% or more over the last assessment, and not because of new construction or improvements, the burden of proof moves to the assessor. Hold on to your increase notice, and gather photographs, repair estimates or recent sales of similar homes to show the value is too high. Paper evidence beats a phone call.

The State Tax Commission is the next level, available under RSMo 138.430 inside the chapter's time limit or 30 days after the board's final action, whichever is later. It corrects assessments it finds unlawful, unfair, improper, arbitrary or capricious. Disputes over exemption or the wrong taxing location belong in circuit court, filed within 30 days.

Delinquent land sale in August

Delinquent parcels go on the auction block every year on August's fourth Monday, 10:00 a.m., at the Dallas County Annex Building in Buffalo. RSMo 140.150 puts the next sale in August 2027. Until a parcel actually sells, you can still pay the taxes, penalty, interest and costs.

  • A bidder must live in Missouri or appoint an agent who does.
  • The sale notice warns that a parcel may carry hazardous waste, liens or condemned buildings.
  • The owner has a year after the sale to redeem.
  • Bid money above the tax amount earns no interest.

The Collector has to mail the recorded owner a first class notice before parcels are advertised, and a certified notice too when assessed value is over $1,000. Missing the letter does not wipe out the tax. If you are behind, ask the Assessor which mailing address is on file.

Other Collector services for new owners

Beyond tax bills, the Collector's desk also handles utility taxes, merchant and auctioneer license fees and duplicate receipt fees, and writes tax exempt waivers where they apply.

A person arriving from another state has 30 days to obtain Missouri plates and a Missouri driver's license. The Collector's site lists what plates require: title or registration, proof of insurance, a Missouri inspection certificate, and either a validated tax receipt from the Collector or a non-assessment clearance from the Assessor. Someone coming from another Missouri county should request an assessment sheet from the Assessor before March 1 to avoid a penalty. Your own buyer may be a newcomer like this, so pass these steps along.

Selling a house in Dallas County

Buffalo is both the seat and the largest city, and the county is part of the Springfield metro area.

Gather a few things before listing: the latest statement for each parcel, the legal description from the deed, and the Collector's current payoff. If you own personal property such as a vehicle in the county, tax on it follows its own cycle, so settle that account separately from the land. Closing goes faster when the tax record is clean, because a buyer's lender will want to see it, and the title company can order the figures for you.

When your house sells, have the title company request a current statement from the Collector and settle the year's tax at the table. If the transfer comes after the November mailing, let the Collector know where the new bill should go. Back taxes on a parcel have to be paid before the office takes the current year, so a house with several unpaid years needs the whole stack cleared before closing. Ask the Collector for each year's balance separately, then add them up with the title company before you set a closing date. That way no unpaid year surprises you at the table. Cash Home Buyers can buy a house in that position and let the closing agent pay the Collector from the price.

Frequently asked questions

When does Dallas County tax become delinquent?

Once December 31 passes. A statement can be paid on receipt, and mailed checks need a postmark of that day or sooner. Anything later is returned without penalty and interest. If November ends with no statement, phone (417) 345-7836.

What are the Collector's office hours and address?

Find it in the Dallas County Administration Building at 102 S Cedar Street, Buffalo, MO 65622. It opens weekdays 8:00 to 12:00 and 1:00 to 4:00, and mail goes to PO Box 529.

Which office sets assessed value?

That is the Assessor, (417) 345-8774. Since the Collector bills from the Assessor's records, take value, owner name, vehicle and legal description questions there.

What date ends the window to appeal to the board of equalization?

RSMo 137.275 sets it at the second Monday in July. You can attend, send an attorney or agent, or submit a letter, and the County Clerk can give you the hearing schedule.

When is the delinquent land sale?

Every year on the fourth Monday of August, and the next is in August 2027. Owners may pay before the sale and then have a year to redeem.

The two courthouse offices

Everything runs out of 100 West Franklin in Clinton, ZIP 64735. The assessor, at 660-885-7212, opens early: 7:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on weekdays, with evening or weekend visits by appointment. The assessor's page also links the county GIS map.

The bill itself comes from the Henry County Treasurer, who doubles as Ex Officio Collector of Revenue. Reach that desk at 660-885-7207, by fax at 660-885-7259 or at collector@henrycountymo.net. A question about worth belongs to the assessor, and a question about what you owe belongs to the collector. Having your parcel number in hand speeds up either call, and the GIS map helps you find it if the bill is not at hand.

Housing and land in Henry County

West-central Missouri's Henry County counts 22,671 residents and 10,750 housing units, with Clinton as the seat and biggest town. Owners live in 75.0 percent of the homes. The median owned home is worth $160,600, a mortgage runs about $1,212 monthly, rent is $768 and household income is $57,926. Builders took out just 18 permits in 2025, so most buyers are shopping resale.

Hilly timber and creek ground near the Truman Reservoir draws hunters and anglers. A shoreline or wooded parcel gets marketed differently from a Clinton or Windsor town lot, and its assessment class can differ too, since farmland and residential ground carry different rates. Buyers also ask about the school district, which the assessor's parcel record shows.

How taxable value is figured

A home is taxed on 19 percent of its market value, farmland on 12 percent and commercial property on 32 percent (RSMo 137.115). New values arrive in odd-numbered years and stay put through the even year that follows.

  • A home value that rises over 15 percent, excluding new construction, needs an inspection on site.
  • Written notice goes to the owner, who has a month or more to ask for an interior look.
  • A drive-by does not satisfy the law.

On appeal of such an increase, RSMo 138.060 makes the assessor prove the figure is no higher than what the house would sell for.

Appealing a value, step by step

  1. Pull your parcel record and check the acreage, buildings and classification against the house.
  2. Phone 660-885-7212, ask how the number was reached and offer sale prices of similar properties.
  3. If the call settles nothing, file with the Board of Equalization by the second Monday in July.
  4. If the Board's letter goes against you, take it to the State Tax Commission within 30 days of the letter. Filing is online, by email to Legal@stc.mo.gov or by post to PO Box 146, Jefferson City, MO 65102-0146, and the Commission will tell you what else it needs.
  5. Keep paying on time. A late bill draws a penalty no matter what an appeal says.

A company, trust or estate must use a lawyer to file. Send the tax bill or the Board letter first and hold the rest of your evidence. An agreed value signed with the assessor shuts the door on further appeals, so read any such paper twice before signing. The local forms are available at 660-885-7212.

Tax calendar for a seller

When the house changes hands

Close in March and you are still the person the county looked to for that year's assessment. Only the sales contract splits the year, with the buyer repaying you for the later months or you crediting the buyer for the earlier ones. The county stays out of that math.

Ask the title company to explain the proration clause and name the tax year it covers. Then call the collector to learn if an older year is still open, since a leftover balance is the usual snag at closing.

Back taxes and the August sale

Delinquent land can be sold on the fourth Monday of August. RSMo 140.150 allows an owner to halt the sale by paying tax, penalty, interest and costs to the collector first. The notice rides first class mail to the owner of record. If it goes astray, the sale still goes ahead.

Call 660-885-7207 for a payoff before listing and hand the number to your title company. If you dispute the value, RSMo 139.031 permits payment under protest: the full amount before delinquency, a written statement to the collector and a circuit court suit within ninety days.

Unpaid years, an inherited title or tenants do not rule out a sale. Cash buyers skip the lender appraisal, and the payoff is deducted from your proceeds when you close.

A sale timeline that avoids tax surprises

Plan from the closing date backward. Get the payoff and parcel record first. Close to the date, check once more with the collector for any earlier year. At the table, your title company settles with the collector out of your proceeds and splits this year as the contract says, then hands you the receipt.

Listing in the fall puts you near the mailing of bills and the December 31 due date. Listing in spring means the January 1 assessment already belongs to you as the holder, so the contract should say how the buyer will repay your share. Whatever the season, a written payoff and a receipt are worth more than a verbal promise from either side.

A vacant, inherited or tenant-occupied house follows the same steps. Pay what is owed, get the receipt and file it with the closing papers. If a late bill is part of the story, remember that the penalty starts the day after the due date, so a payment that is only a few days behind still costs extra.

What to keep in your listing folder

Keep the assessor's parcel record, the collector's current balance and any notice about a changed value in one folder. A buyer's agent will ask what the land is classed as, what the bill is and whether anything is overdue, and those three papers answer all of it.

If your value jumped, note the notice date and remember that the Board window shuts on the second Monday in July. Calling the assessor early in the week leaves room to fix a problem before a closing date.

Frequently asked questions

Who sends the Henry County bill?

The Treasurer, acting as Ex Officio Collector of Revenue, at 100 West Franklin in Clinton. Phone 660-885-7207.

What share of my home's value is taxed?

Homes count at nineteen percent of true value. The district levies are then applied to that smaller assessed figure.

Is there a grace period after December 31?

A mailed payment is judged by its postmark, and the collector adds a penalty starting January 1. Ask the collector's office whether an exception applies to you.

Can the county sell my house for back taxes?

It can, once the taxes are delinquent, at the sale held the fourth Monday of August. You stop it by paying everything owed before that day.

How do I reach the Henry County assessor?

Phone 660-885-7212 or go to 100 West Franklin in Clinton on weekdays. The office opens at 7:30 a.m. and will arrange visits at other times.

About $100 million in tax revenue moves through the Collector every year on its way to 33 taxing districts. Besides printing statements, the office issues Merchant and Manufacturer licenses and conducts the August delinquent tax sale. The Assessor, an elected official, maintains a roll of more than 40,000 real parcels and over 110,000 articles of personal property.

Selling in Buchanan County

St. Joseph, the seat, had 72,473 residents in 2020, and the county runs along the Missouri River in Missouri's northwest corner. By about July 1 the Assessor completes the roll and hands it to the County Clerk. Districts set budgets and levies near the end of September, and the Assessor plays no role in that step.

Payment due date and ways to pay

Bills are mailed in the first week of November. The Collector wants payment when you receive yours, and December 31 divides on time from late. To count, a payment must arrive by that date or bear an official U.S. Postal Service postmark. Metered postage from a private machine doesn't qualify. State law on mailed payments is in RSMo 139.100.

Nothing in the mailbox by the end of November? Ask the office for a copy, because a missing bill doesn't waive interest or penalties. Online payers get a mailed receipt in three to five business days, so pay in person if you need one within seven. Accepted: cash, check, American Express, Discover, MasterCard and Visa. If Buchanan County taxes go unpaid

The Collector applies money to old debt first. Delinquent real estate and personal property tax must be cleared before any payment counts toward the current year. After December 31, use the payment schedule printed on the statement.

Once land is in the back tax book, RSMo 140.100 adds a penalty of 18 percent of that year's delinquency, or no more than 2 percent a month if the owner redeems ahead of the sale. Under RSMo 140.150, delinquent land can be sold on the fourth Monday of August. Beforehand the Collector must send the recorded owner a first class letter, plus a certified one if assessed value exceeds $1,000. Until the sale, you may pay the tax, penalty and costs and keep the property.

Tax relief for seniors

The county's website points to two programs. First, the state Property Tax Credit returns up to $750 to residents who are 65 or older, totally disabled or disabled by military service, or who are 60 or older and draw surviving spouse Social Security. Income, counting Social Security, must stay at or under $25,000 for one filer and $27,000 for a married couple. Call 573-751-3505 at the Department of Revenue, or 800-877-6881 to get Form MO-PTC.

Second, in September 2024 the County Commission opted into the Senior Citizen Homestead Property Tax Credit (RSMo 137.1050). Ask the courthouse when the next application window opens.
