Taxes and recording when you sell

Selling doesn't cancel the year's bill, so agree on who pays what before closing. Get the parcel's balance from the Collector, keeping in mind that old taxes clear first. Name, mailing address and legal description issues go to the Assessor instead.

The Recorder of Deeds is in Room 103 of the same building at 411 Jules Street, phone 816-271-1437. Nothing is recorded after 4:00 PM. Documents delivered later are filed in the order received at 8:00 AM the next business day, a real concern if a closing drags near December 31 or a payoff deadline. The Recorder can't draft a deed or give legal advice, so lean on a title company or attorney.

A cash buyer removes the lender payoff from the timeline. The tax balance and the 4:00 PM recording cutoff still apply, so schedule signing in the morning when you can.

Preparing a Buchanan County house for sale

Most tax trouble at a closing can be spotted weeks ahead. Work through this list once you decide to sell.

  1. Call 816-271-1401 and ask the Collector for the balance on your parcel, including any older year.
  2. Check the statement for the right name, mailing address and legal description. If something is off, the Assessor at 816-271-1520 fixes it.
  3. Ask whether you have a senior credit or freeze that will end when the house sells, so the buyer knows what to expect on their own bill.
  4. Tell the title company about any payment you made online, since the mailed receipt takes three to five business days.
  5. Plan the signing so the deed reaches the Recorder before 4:00 PM.

If a statement hasn't come by the end of November, don't wait. Ask for a copy, because the December 31 deadline and its penalties still apply to the owner of record.

How to appeal your assessment

The Assessor's office is the place to ask how your value was reached. Not satisfied? File with the Board of Equalization by the second Monday in July. After the board rules you have 30 days to go to the State Tax Commission, a right set out in RSMo 138.430.

Pay without protest and skip both appeals, and that year's assessment is final, though next year's can be challenged. An LLC, trust, estate or corporation needs an attorney to appeal to the State Tax Commission. Bring comparable sales or an appraisal to any hearing.

In Room 123 at 411 Jules Street, St. Joseph, open weekdays 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM. Call 816-271-1401.

Yes, using the county's Pay/View Taxes application. It adds a convenience fee that the Collector neither sets nor keeps. For a receipt in under seven days, pay in person.

Each August. State law sets delinquent land sales for the fourth Monday of the month.

Who bills and who values

Cole County splits tax duties between the Assessor, who puts a value on each parcel, and the Collector of Revenue, who mails statements and banks the payments. Find the Collector in Room 100 of the Courthouse Annex, 311 E High Street, Jefferson City 65101. The number is 573-634-9124, and staff answer weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. A drop box by the High Street entrance of the Annex is always accessible.

Hearing dates for the Board of Equalization come from the County Clerk. Above the county, the Missouri State Tax Commission oversees assessors and takes appeals once the local board has ruled. Take value complaints to the Assessor and billing problems to the Collector. A homeowner who walks into the wrong office usually gets pointed across the hall, so decide first whether your problem is the number or the bill. Your payment is divided among the state, municipalities, rural fire districts, the public library and the school districts.

Payment deadlines and late costs

You may pay a real estate bill from the day it reaches you, and the final date is December 31. Mailed checks count by postmark. Statements are mailed through November. Should yours be missing by the second week of December, the Collector wants a call, since a lost bill does not lift the tax or the late fees.

  • First-year delinquency can add as much as 25% in charges.
  • Tax sticks to the parcel, which means the next owner inherits any balance still open.
  • When a lender pays your tax from escrow, pass the bill along to the lender.
  • If a bill arrives for a house you have sold, send the Collector the new owner's name and address.

Online, cards carry a 2.25% convenience fee and e-checks a $1.75 fee, with 5 to 7 days for an e-check to clear. Other routes are the phone at 855-568-0066, dropping by the counter or mailing a check. A postmark of December 31 is timely, and the drop box stays open until midnight that night. Counter payments can be cash, personal check, cashier's check, bank draft, money order or card, and a single check can cover several bills.

How the amount is worked out

The math is assessed value divided by 100, then times the levy. Assessed value is only a slice of market value, and the size of the slice follows the parcel's class.

Class of real estateShare of value assessed
Residential19%
Agricultural12%
Commercial32%

Levies come from voters and the taxing districts, and the Assessor's site links a rate sheet. The county's real estate tax page walks through the method, and the Collector's staff will explain it by phone. If you want a rough bill for the house you are selling, first learn which taxing districts include the parcel, because the combined levy changes from place to place.

How to challenge a Cole County valuation

An informal chat with the Assessor is the first move. It is optional and offered on weekdays during office hours. Come with proof of market value, such as photographs, an inspection report, a recent appraisal or nearby sales. In the county's words, the Assessor's job is to keep values in step with the current market.

A formal review happens at the Board of Equalization, and the filing cutoff under RSMo 137.275 is the second Monday in July. Members include the County Commissioners, an Assessor who does not vote and appointees, with two city appointees added for parcels in Jefferson City. The County Clerk keeps the record and mails each taxpayer a written decision.

If you remain unhappy, take the matter to the State Tax Commission. RSMo 138.430 sets the appeal period at the one stated in that chapter or 30 days after the local board finishes, whichever ends later. Those sessions are usually in September and October with a single Administrative Hearing Officer. An appraisal is expected, and hiring a lawyer is up to you.

Land sold for unpaid tax

After three delinquent years, a parcel qualifies for the county's certificate sale. The auction opens at 10 in the morning at the Cole County Courthouse, and RSMo 140.150 places it on the fourth Monday in August statewide. Pay the Collector the tax, penalty, interest and costs ahead of time and the parcel comes out of the sale.

  • The Jefferson City News Tribune publishes the parcel list three weeks running before the sale.
  • A winning bid earns a certificate of purchase, and the original owner can redeem for a year after the sale.
  • Existing liens outlast both the sale and the redemption period.
  • A bidder who wins and then fails to pay faces a 25% penalty and a prosecuting attorney fee.

A seller who is behind can ask the Collector for a current payoff. Nothing is paid to that office at the sale itself, so get any payoff amount in writing by way of the title company.

Who pays when a house changes hands

Ownership in the fall decides who pays the November bill, so after a mid-year sale the buyer does. Closing normally prorates the tax and gives the buyer a credit for the days or months the seller owned the place. The buyer pays the full bill by December 31.

Central Missouri holds Cole County, just south of the Missouri River, and Jefferson City is both the seat and the state capital. The July 1, 2025 estimates list 77,908 people and 33,956 housing units. Owners occupy 67.9% of units, the 2020 to 2024 median value is $229,600, and median household income is $74,876. Median rent is $834, and 154 building permits were issued in 2025.

A tidy way to prepare: ask the Collector for your parcel balance, and check the taxing districts shown on your last statement. The title company can then print the tax line for your settlement statement, and the Collector only needs the new owner's mailing address once the sale is done. Cash Home Buyers can purchase a house with back taxes or a lien problem, with the closing agent clearing the balance out of the price, so nothing is left to chase afterward.

Pull together a short folder before the listing goes live: your latest statement, the Collector's payoff figure, any Assessor notice showing the value, and notes from any informal talk with the Assessor. Buyers' agents often ask what the tax will be, and a folder like this lets you answer from paper instead of memory.

If you escrow, tell your lender about the sale so it can send any leftover cushion your way. Keep the closing statement with your records, along with a copy of the paid receipt, in case a question about the year's tax comes up months later.

Frequently asked questions

When does Cole County property tax become late?

Right after December 31. You can pay any time after the bill arrives, mail counts by postmark, and the courthouse drop box is good until midnight on the last day. A first delinquent year can add up to 25% in charges.

Will the Collector mail me a bill?

Yes, during November. Nothing by the second week of December? Phone 573-634-9124. A lost bill changes nothing about what you owe or the late fees.

What is the last day to appeal to the Board of Equalization?

The second Monday in July, with the filing made through the County Clerk. A talk with the Assessor can come before that.

Who owes the tax after a mid-year sale?

The buyer is billed for the full amount in December and normally gets a proration credit at closing. The Collector receives nothing at the table. If the bill still comes to you, mail the Collector the buyer's address.

How many years of unpaid tax lead to a sale?

Three years. Then the parcel may be offered at the August certificate sale, though the owner can still pay beforehand or redeem during the year that follows.

Johnson County housing snapshot

Warrensburg is both the seat and the largest city of Johnson County, a western Missouri county bordering Lafayette, Pettis, Henry, Cass and Jackson counties and tied into the wider Kansas City area. Holden and Knob Noster round out the cities. In 2025 the county counted 56,670 residents, 4.9% more than in 2020. Owners live in 63.5% of homes. The typical owned home is valued at $235,700, and typical gross rent is $932.

Seven public school districts cover the county, and each adds a levy to bills inside its boundaries. Buyers will want to know which one serves your house.

Offices that handle property tax

Responsibility splits three ways. Value and the owner of record are the Assessor's job. Each taxing district picks its own rate. Billing, payment and the hand-off of funds to those districts belong to the Collector.

  • Assessor: Johnson County South Annex, 1310 S Maguire St, Suite B, Warrensburg, MO 64093, phone 660-747-9822.
  • Collector: 1310 S Maguire St, Suite A, Warrensburg, MO 64093, phone 660-747-5531.
  • Thanksgiving: county administrative offices will be closed on Thursday and Friday, November 26 and 27, 2026.

The Assessor has no role in rates, collections or what schools and fire districts receive. If you wonder why a levy went up, ask the district that charges it.

How market value becomes a tax bill

The county publishes its formula. Multiply market value by the adjustment factor for the property class to get assessed value, divide by 100, multiply by a district's rate, and total the districts.

Johnson County assessment factors
Property classShare of market value assessed
Residential19%
Commercial32%
Agricultural12%

Which districts apply depends on where your parcel lies: school, fire, ambulance and city.

Real estate values are redone in odd-numbered years under Missouri law, and the next round is 2027. A jump of $500 or more in assessed value triggers a mailed Change in Assessed Value Notice, usually in June, and even-numbered years can bring one too. Since no tax estimate is included, call the Assessor if you want one.

Disputing your value

The county outlines three steps. First, read the notice for factual errors. Second, if you have proof of a different value or of a data mistake, ask the Assessor for an informal hearing. Third, when that goes nowhere, submit a Property Assessment Appeal Form to get in front of the Board of Equalization. Hearings are by appointment, and contact details are printed on every mailed notice.

Filing with the Board closes on the second Monday of July (July 12 in 2027). The Assessor or County Clerk can tell you where the form goes and whether any extension applies. If the Board rules against you, the State Tax Commission is next, and you have 30 days counted from the date of the decision letter.

  • You may owe the tax while an appeal is pending, and balances left after December 31 accrue interest and penalties.
  • Signing a value agreement with the Assessor during a Board appeal settles the matter for good, with no Commission appeal after it.
  • Appeals to the Commission by an LLC, trust, estate or corporation need an attorney.

Due dates and how to find your balance

Bills leave the Collector's office in late October. Delinquency starts after December 31, so mailed checks must bear a postmark of that day or sooner. Envelopes with a later postmark come back unprocessed, unless the late fees are enclosed.

Your balance is on the county's Search Taxes page. Choose Real Estate and type in a name, street address or mailing address; the first number returned is your parcel number. Under Missouri statute 140.100, land in the back tax book takes an 18 percent penalty for each year of delinquency, so a lapsed bill climbs quickly.

Escrowed owners get new figures through their mortgage company, but the county notes that getting the bill paid on time is still the owner's duty.

Senior property tax credit

Ordinance 25-01, passed by the County Commission on March 17, 2025, set up a Senior Real Estate Tax Credit under section 137.1050. It is open to homeowners age 62 and over and applies to the primary residence, measured by how much tax rises after a starting credit year.

  • The application period has been April 1 to June 30. The Collector can tell you when the next one begins.
  • Not covered: agricultural and commercial property, personal property, voter-approved bond levies and the State Blind Pension levy.
  • Every tax on the homestead has to be paid up.
  • Your value is not frozen; reassessment still happens in odd years.

Sellers should know the credit follows the person. A buyer does not inherit it, and a homeowner who buys elsewhere starts over with a new application and a new starting year.

When unpaid taxes pile up

Three years behind puts a parcel on the list for the yearly tax certificate sale, which takes place on the fourth Monday of August, 10 a.m., at 301 W Market Street in Warrensburg. Notice of the list runs in a local newspaper for three weeks before that.

What a bidder gets is a tax lien and no ownership. Redemption is open to the owner of record and to anyone with a recorded lien or deed of trust, for one year and then until a collector's deed is issued. The price is the bid plus 10% annual interest, and 8% on later years' tax the buyer covered. If 18 months pass after the sale with no collector's deed, the buyer's lien is gone.

Any surplus above the opening bid is held by the County Treasurer. To claim it, an owner or lienholder has ninety days after redemption ends to file with the county commission; after that it goes to the schools.

Selling with taxes owed

A tax balance alone will not stop a sale, because the title company can ask for a payoff figure and take it out of your proceeds. Here is the order of work.

  1. Phone the Collector, 660-747-5531, and request a payoff figure with penalty and interest built in.
  2. A house more than a year behind should have that figure in hand before it is listed.
  3. A house close to three years behind is the urgent case, since it can land in the August sale.
  4. Hand the written figure to the title company so the settlement statement matches it.

A cash sale can close fast enough to pay the arrears before the sale date, and the proceeds cover the bill the same way they would in any other closing.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay Johnson County real estate tax?

At the Collector's office, 1310 S Maguire St, Suite A in Warrensburg, or through the county's online payment link. The phone is 660-747-5531. A mailed payment needs a December 31 postmark.

What is the Johnson County residential assessment rate?

Nineteen percent of market value. Commercial property is 32% and agricultural property is 12%. District rates then apply to that assessed value.

When will Johnson County reassess my house again?

In 2027, because Missouri reassesses real estate in odd-numbered years. If assessed value rises by $500 or more, a notice usually comes by mail in June.

Does the Johnson County senior tax credit pass to the buyer?

No. It stays with the applicant. A buyer who is 62 or older would need a new application, and a seller who moves must apply again for the new home.

How long before Johnson County sells a home for unpaid tax?

A parcel with three years of delinquent tax must be offered at the sale on the fourth Monday in August. The owner can redeem during the next year by paying the bid plus 10% annual interest.

Laclede County housing and context

Laclede County is a rural Ozarks county in south central Missouri. Lebanon holds the courthouse and is the only big city, and a stretch of the Mark Twain National Forest lies inside the county line. Smaller incorporated places include Conway, Richland, Phillipsburg, Stoutland and Evergreen. Population was 36,943 in July 2025.

The median owner-occupied home is worth $168,400, and 68.2% of homes are lived in by their owners, out of 16,211 housing units. Figure out whether your house is within a city limit or out on a county road before listing, because that changes the levies on your bill. Five public school districts have campuses here. The one serving your address adds its own levy, so tell buyers which it is.

A paid-off house has no escrow account to pay for you. The statement from the collector is your only reminder, so an heir to a house with no loan should mark the due date on a calendar.

Which office does what

Worth is the Assessor's call; billing is the Collector of Revenue's. The collector's office works strictly from the assessor's records and has no power to change a bill. Mistakes in acreage, owner name or parcel description therefore go to the Assessor at (417) 532-7163.

The Collector also handles merchant license fees and railroad and utility tax, and distributes money to schools, road districts, fire protection entities and other local subdivisions. Mortgage companies send escrow payments to the same counter.

The collector's website finds a bill by owner name, parcel number, street address or account number, and shows payment history. Pull up your parcel ahead of listing to see which years are settled.

When bills arrive and how to pay

Once the County Clerk hands over the tax books in late October, the office starts printing, and statements go out in November. The due date is December 31. You get one statement for real estate and another for personal property, and a single check can pay both.

Counter hours are 8am to 4pm, Monday through Friday, except state and federal holidays. For payments after December 31, the delinquency schedule on your statement applies, and the office will quote the penalty on request.

  • At the counter: cash, personal check, money order or cashier's check.
  • By mail: a check in the return envelope, and never cash.
  • By card, on the website or over the phone, plus a convenience fee.
  • In the drop box at the Second Street courthouse entrance, usable at any hour.

Your paid receipt returns by mail after processing. A late payment left in the drop box without its penalty is sent back.

Property tax calendar

In a typical year, the dates run like this.

A year of Laclede County property tax dates
WhenWhat happens
Late OctoberStatements are printed once the tax books arrive

Installment plan and senior credit

Spreading the bill out is possible for most owners. Under the Collector's prepay plan you make ten equal payments based on last year's tax, an eleventh payment settles whatever is left, and the money comes out of your bank account automatically. A delinquent account or a parcel paid through lender escrow is not eligible. The sign-up number is (417) 532-4301.

The senior credit is a different tool. It holds the homestead real estate tax at its first-year level. One home only, and you must live there. Renewal comes yearly, from April 1 through the last Friday in May. Year one always shows a zero credit since earlier years are never refunded. The Collector can say when the next application period starts.

Because it freezes the tax rather than removing it, the tax stays on the home. A seller already enrolled should ask what becomes of the credit at a change of ownership.

What if my value is too high?

The order is Assessor, then the county board of equalization, then the State Tax Commission. Your appeal must reach the board by the second Monday in July. The board's letter starts a 30-day clock for going to the Commission.

Disputing a value does not put you behind on the bill. If you protest, the Commission's guidance is to mail the entire payment to the collector, label it a protest and enclose your written reasons and the market value you claim. A postmark on or before December 31 counts.

Estates, trusts, LLCs and corporations cannot file with the Commission without a lawyer, which is worth remembering for anyone settling a relative's estate ahead of a sale.

The tax certificate sale

In August a bidder may pay your delinquent tax and walk away with a certificate of purchase instead of a deed. It happens on the fourth Monday at 10 a.m., at the courthouse, 200 N. Adams in Lebanon, following three weeks of newspaper notice. If you pay the taxes, penalty, interest and costs before the bidding starts, the parcel comes off the list.

To redeem after a sale, the owner pays the certificate's base amount plus 10% annual interest, along with any later tax the buyer paid, at the same interest. The Collector asks for a day's notice and suggests allowing 20 minutes.

When the year is up, the holder may seek a collector's deed, but only after certified-mail notices go to the owner and lienholders at least 90 days earlier. Liens survive the sale itself. Bid money above the taxes and costs belongs to the owner of record.

Selling with back taxes

Owing tax does not rule out a closing; the sale price pays it off. Three steps get it done.

  1. Get an exact payoff from the collector.
  2. Pass that number to the title company.
  3. Have the closing pay the collector from the price.

A few cases need extra care.

  • If you bought the house before October, the statement may have gone to the previous owner, so ask them and the collector.
  • If the August sale is close, pay the balance before that date.
  • Tell the collector about the sale if you use the installment plan or the senior credit.
  • Call the Assessor about a wrong value well before July.

Written payoff figures protect you if the amount shifts before the closing date. With a cash buyer there is no lender sign-off to wait for, so the title company can pay the collector as soon as it has the number.

Frequently asked questions

Is the Laclede County property tax deadline December 31?

Yes. Statements arrive in November and are due December 31. Payment after that date follows the delinquency schedule on the statement.

Which office fixes an error in my Laclede County parcel record?

The Assessor, at (417) 532-7163. The collector cannot change a bill, since it must collect from the assessor's records.

Can I pay Laclede County property tax by card?

Yes. Cards work online or by phone, with a convenience fee. The office also takes cash, checks and money orders, and a courthouse drop box is open all day.

When must I appeal a Laclede County value?

The county board of equalization needs your appeal by the second Monday in July. The State Tax Commission allows 30 days from the date of the board's letter.

Is it possible to close on a Laclede County home with back tax owed?

Yes. Get a written payoff from the collector so the title company can pay it from your proceeds. If the August sale is near, clearing the balance first keeps the parcel off the list.

Statements go out in early November and are payable the day they arrive. After December 31 they are delinquent. Without a statement by Thanksgiving, phone the Collector at (660) 259-6171.

Dates to know through the year

The county tax year follows a steady pattern, and a sale that falls on the wrong side of one of these dates can cost you.

  • Second Monday in July: cutoff for filing with the county board of equalization.

Reading your statement

Real estate and personal property can arrive as separate statements. Every district with an approved levy shows up on them, which is why a school district, a fire district and the library each take a slice of one payment. The Collector divides the money among them each month, so no one of those bodies will fix your bill for you.

Check the acreage, address and owner name against your deed before paying. Any error is the Assessor's to fix, and it costs less to fix one before a buyer's title company spots it. Put each year's printed receipt in your sale file. Open with a conversation with the Assessor. When it fails, file with the county board of equalization by the second Monday in July at the latest. After the board, the State Tax Commission takes appeals filed within 30 days of the board's letter date.

Send the whole amount to the collector by December 31, label it a protest, and include a written statement of your reasons and your idea of market value. If you bought less than 30 days after the county mailed the statement, or never heard about an increase, you may skip the board and go straight to the Commission.

Delinquent tax sale

Every August the Collector runs a sale of delinquent real estate. Missouri's tax sale rules are in Chapter 140 of the state statutes, and the winning bidder receives a certificate of purchase rather than an immediate deed.

Call the Collector for this year's date, the list of parcels and the amount needed to take yours off it, and ask which tax years put a parcel on the list.

When more than one year is open, ask the Collector to break the balance out by tax year. A seller who closes first avoids the sale altogether. The title company can pay the open balance from the proceeds at closing.

What to gather before selling a house that owes tax

Pull together a current statement and a written payoff from the Collector, and make sure both the real estate and personal property accounts are clear. Because the office refuses partial payment, the payoff has to cover the whole statement.

  3. Print your paid receipt from the county site.
  4. Agree with the buyer on how the current year will be split.

Bring a copy of the payoff letter and the paid receipts to the closing so the settlement statement matches the Collector's numbers.

In the courthouse at 1001 Main Street in Lexington. The phone is (660) 259-6158, and the email is assessor@lafayettecountymo.gov.

Missouri adds a penalty to unpaid taxes after the delinquency date (RSMo 139.100). Before paying late, ask the Collector at (417) 223-7408 what penalty and interest percentages apply. Mailed payments count on the postmark date.

Each August the Collector holds the delinquent sale. A parcel with old unpaid years can head toward auction long before an owner notices.

How do I contest my McDonald County value?

Start by phoning the Assessor, (417) 223-4361, to request an informal review. Gather recent nearby sales, contractor repair quotes or photos that support a lower number, and write down the date and name of each person you speak with so you can follow up. Also ask when the local equalization board accepts filings.

If the board leaves your value alone, RSMo 138.430 lets you take the case to the State Tax Commission. The filing is due on the statutory date or 30 days after the board's final action, whichever comes later. Once an appeal is filed, the contested taxes are held in a separate fund instead of reaching the taxing bodies.

A second route is paying under protest. RSMo 139.031: settle the full bill before delinquency and hand the collector a written explanation of your objection. A protest becomes void if you file no circuit court suit against the collector within ninety days. An appeal already pending at the State Tax Commission stands in for that suit.

Tax relief for owners

State revenue officials administer the Property Tax Credit Claim, nicknamed the circuit breaker. Some seniors and people who are 100 percent disabled get back part of what they paid in property tax or rent. The ceiling is $1,100 for owner-occupants and $750 for renters, and the exact credit depends on tax paid and household income of every kind. Questions can go to PropertyTaxCredit@dor.mo.gov.

One more break is a homestead exemption for a former prisoner of war who has a total service-connected disability. The home must be the owner's primary residence. Show the assessor the federal disability letter and discharge papers, or a records center letter that confirms the prisoner of war history.

Military personnel living here on orders, with a home of record elsewhere, generally owe no Missouri personal property tax on non-business items.

Selling with taxes owed

Treat the tax bill as a closing line item. Before you list, ask the Collector for the status of each year on the parcel. The closing agent will divide the current year between you and the buyer. Delinquent years can put a parcel in the August sale, so pay old balances first.

  • Check the name and address the Assessor has on record.
  • Request a payoff amount for each parcel in the sale, land and any manufactured home included.
  • Keep the settlement statement, since it shows how that year's tax was divided.
  • A value that seems too high should be raised with the Assessor before the board deadline, not once the sale is done.

Plan the order of calls this way. First phone the Collector for balances. Next ask the Assessor whether the name, address and class on the parcel are right. Then give both figures to the closing agent so the settlement statement matches. If a bill arrives after closing, the statement you saved shows who owed which share, and the Collector can confirm what was paid under the parcel.

Back taxes can stall a financed sale, because the title company wants an open balance resolved first. A cash buyer has no lender waiting on a clean tax record, so closing can move faster. The unpaid amount is still taken out of your proceeds at the table, and the Collector's payoff figure tells you how much.

Frequently asked questions

What date makes a McDonald County tax bill late?

Anything unpaid after December 31. Bills go out the first week of November, and a payment postmarked in January comes back unless late fees are included.

Can I pay half of my bill now and half later?

No. The Collector cannot accept partial payment, though all statements can be paid together with a single check.

What assessment rate applies to a McDonald County house?

Residential property is assessed at 19 percent of market value. Farmland is 12 percent and commercial parcels are 32 percent, before any taxing body applies its levy.

Where do I send an address correction for my tax statement?

Call the Assessor at (417) 223-4361. The Collector's site routes address changes to that office.

When is the delinquent tax sale?

It happens each August at the Collector's office. For the exact date and the parcels offered, call (417) 223-7408.

Dunklin County offices to know

Kennett's courthouse square holds the two elected offices that shape a Dunklin County tax bill. One sets the value and the other sends the bill and cashes the check. Both are at 100 Kennett Court Square, Kennett, MO 63857.

The Collector-Treasurer is in Room 203, phone 573-888-2180, mailing address PO Box 445. The assessor can be reached at 573-888-1409 or 573-888-4771. The recorder of deeds is in Room 204, 573-888-3468.

Money the collector takes in is passed along to every district that levies on the parcel: ambulance, health center, library, schools, state, townships, the road and bridge fund and the sheltered workshop. A city levy is billed separately by the city. Never combine it with a county check.

Housing in the Bootheel

Dunklin County fills part of Missouri's far southeastern Bootheel, with Kennett as seat and largest town. The population estimate is 26,855, a drop of 5.1 percent from 28,292 in April 2020. Of 13,520 housing units, 62.3 percent are owner-occupied. The median owned home is worth $97,600, against median rent of $648.

Values this low keep the yearly tax to a few hundred dollars, but a neglected year can still eat into what a seller walks away with. Houses inside Kennett, Malden, Senath or Clarkton also owe the town, so ask both offices what is open.

How a house gets its taxable value

The assessor lists every taxable parcel annually. New values are set as of January 1 of odd-numbered years and stay in place through the next even year unless the property was improved. Under RSMo 137.115 a house is counted at 19 percent of its true value, cropland at 12 and commercial buildings at 32, and each district's levy runs against that smaller figure.

A residential jump of more than 15 percent, unless it comes from new building, requires an in-person inspection first. Owners can request a look inside and have at least 30 days to make that request. A drive-by does not satisfy the rule.

If you switch a property from farm to residential use, apply to the assessor to have it reclassified. Personal property filings can be made online through the assessor's page.

How to appeal your assessment

The notice comes first. RSMo 137.180 requires the assessor to mail any increase to the record owner's last known address, and in a reassessment year that mailing is due by June 15. If the figure looks wrong, phone the assessor with recent sale prices for similar houses.

The formal venue is the county Board of Equalization (RSMo 138.060), which does not start from a presumption that the assessor is right. The assessor must carry the proof only when a value climbed 15 percent or more without new construction. The filing cutoff is the second Monday in July, which will be July 12 in 2027. The Dunklin County Clerk can tell you where the form goes.

A loss at the Board can go to the State Tax Commission, with a complaint due September 30 or 30 days after the Board's final action, whichever falls later. Property titled to a company, trust or estate must go through an attorney. Send the tax bill or the Board's decision letter with the complaint and save the rest of your evidence until the Commission asks.

Due dates, penalties and collector rules

December 31 is the due date. RSMo 139.100 counts a mailed payment as made on its postmark date, so an envelope stamped that day is timely. Starting January 1 the collector adds the penalty fixed by RSMo 140.100: 18 percent of the year's delinquency, with a monthly cap of 2 percent for land redeemed before the sale.

Know these counter rules before driving to Kennett:

You can pay a disputed bill under protest. Pay all of it before it goes delinquent, put the reasons and your claimed value in writing, and sue the collector inside 90 days as RSMo 139.031 provides. Tax paid by mistake can be refunded if you claim it within three years.

The August tax sale

Each year on the fourth Monday of August, RSMo 140.150 has the collector offer land with taxes unpaid for two years. Parcels that draw no buyer after a third offering can be purchased with the deed issued on the spot.

Up to the day of the sale you can wipe out the debt by paying the tax, penalty, interest and costs. Notice goes out by ordinary mail, with a certified second letter when the assessed value tops $1,000. If the mail never reaches you, the debt still stands.

With old years open on your house, mark that August Monday as the last safe day. Pay ahead of it and the house stays out of the offering.

All three open at 8:30 a.m. and close at 4:30 p.m., so one trip to the square can cover the bill, the value and the deed.

Selling with taxes owed

Request an up-to-date statement in Room 203 before listing. Any earlier year gets paid ahead of this one. Give your closing agent the parcel number and the collector's phone so the payoff matches what the office has on file. Your sales contract, not the county, decides how this year's bill is divided with the buyer.

On the deed side, the recorder's fees changed on August 27, 2026. A one-page document is $26, and each extra page up to 20 pages adds $3. Plats and surveys are priced separately. Missouri counties accept electronic filing through a shared portal, so ask Room 204 if filing online suits your closing.

Liens, tenants or a failing roof can stall a conventional sale of a Kennett-area house. A cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal, and the tax payoff is taken from your proceeds at the closing table.

Who bills Dunklin County property tax?

The Collector-Treasurer's office in Room 203 mails it. The assessor's job ends at the value, and any city tax arrives on a separate bill.

December 31. An envelope postmarked that day is on time, and the 18 percent penalty begins January 1.

Can I pay part of my Dunklin County bill?

No, the counter takes only the whole amount and refuses mixed cash and check. Back years have to be settled before this year's tax is accepted.

When are delinquent Dunklin County houses sold?

Land two years behind is offered on the fourth Monday of August. Paying the tax, penalty and costs before that day pulls it from the list.

Phone the assessor, then file with the Board of Equalization by the second Monday in July. The State Tax Commission hears any further appeal.

Who bills and collects Pike County property tax?

Land, house, vehicle and boat taxes in Pike County are billed and collected by the Collector of Revenue, whose office is at 115 West Main, Bowling Green, MO 63334. Call 573-324-3281. Weekday hours run 8 to 4:30, and the office closes from noon to 1 for lunch outside tax season.

Pike County sits on Missouri's eastern edge along the Mississippi River, and Bowling Green is the seat. Other cities are Clarksville, Curryville, Frankford and Louisiana. An estimated 17,955 people lived here in July 2025, spread over 7,682 housing units. Owners occupy 73.3 percent of the homes in use. Median owned-home value is $146,000, rent is $778 monthly and household income is $54,989. With only 20 building permits in 2025, this is a small market dominated by owners.

With home values that modest, one delinquent year can be a large share of what a house is worth. The timing of the bill matters more here than the rate itself.

When bills are mailed and due

November 1 is the mailing date for statements. A bill that fails to arrive by mid-November deserves a call to the collector, since the tax and late charges apply either way. A December 31 postmark keeps you on time. Later postmarks come back unprocessed unless interest and penalty are enclosed.

Neither partial nor pro-rated payments are taken. On a parcel with several unpaid years, the oldest is applied first under RSMo 140.110. A single check may cover multiple bills, provided every statement goes in with it.

Each January 1 is the assessment date. A house is counted at 19 percent of market value, farmland at 12 percent of what it produces, and all other real estate at 32 percent. Reviews come every two years, and state law wants values within 5 percent of the market.

Call the Pike County Assessor at 573-324-3261 before the county board opens its July hearings. If that fails, the State Tax Commission appeal is due by September 30 or thirty days after the board mails its letter.

The auction runs at 10 a.m. on the fourth Monday of August, on the south side of the courthouse. Only parcels with a third year of delinquent tax must be offered, and an owner can pay before the sale to remove the parcel.

Property tax offices in Salem

The courthouse at 400 N. Main Street, Salem, MO 65560 holds most of the offices you will deal with.

  • County Clerk: 573-729-4144. The Clerk schedules Board of Equalization appointments.
  • Recorder of Deeds: 112 E. Fifth Street, Suite 2, 573-729-2198.

The Assessor values taxable property. The Collector bills it, receives payment, passes the money to the taxing districts and also handles escrow payments sent in by mortgage holders. View and pay statements at dentcountycollector.com. The Assessor's GIS map pulls up a parcel by street address, owner or parcel number, and a yearly subscription is available for people who need property data or maps regularly.

Vehicle owners should know that new plates require proof that the previous year's personal property tax was paid, shown by a paid receipt or a waiver from the Assessor. The Collector also takes county merchant license fees and sends the paid personal property list to the License Bureau each month.

When bills go out and when tax is due

The Collector sends real estate and personal property bills by November 8. They are due by the end of December, and a penalty kicks in on January 1. The money is then split among 22 political subdivisions that hold certified levies, among them schools, roads and fire districts. The Collector also bills tax on state assessed utilities such as railroads, pipelines and electric lines.

  • Paying before the new year avoids the penalty, and the Collector can show you the late schedule.
  • With a lender escrowing your tax, confirm the lender really got the bill.
  • Personal property has a separate schedule. Owners list it with the Assessor between January 1 and March 1, and lateness can cost up to $105.00 under RSMo 137.280.
  • Newcomers from another Missouri county bring their last paid personal property receipt to open a Dent County account, and anyone new to the state must open one too.

After a sale, either you or the title company should report the buyer's name and mailing address to the Collector, so the next statement is not mailed to you.

How a house is assessed

The statutory assessment date is January 1, and more than 11,000 parcels are valued as of that day. Real estate falls into three subclasses: residential at 19% of market value, agricultural at 12% of production value and everything else at 32% of true value in money. A full reassessment lands in odd-numbered years, and new construction or additions are added each year.

To get the tax, divide the assessed figure by 100 and multiply by the combined levy of the districts over your parcel. Either office can look that levy up.

How to appeal a valuation

Your first call should be to the Assessor, to learn how the value was reached. The State Tax Commission oversees assessors, and its field representatives visit Dent County monthly and spot-review properties each year. Not convinced? The Board of Equalization is next, and RSMo 137.275 closes filing on the second Monday in July.

Hearings are booked through the County Clerk. Under RSMo 138.060 the board rules summarily, and the assessor's valuation gets no presumption of being right. If your valuation rose 15% or more over the last assessment for reasons other than new construction or improvements, the assessor must show the value is not above true market value. Bring last cycle's notice, photos and any appraisal or sales evidence.

After that, RSMo 138.430 sends you to the State Tax Commission. You have 30 days from the board's final action or until the chapter's own deadline, whichever is later, and because the right flows from the board's decision, the board hearing has to happen first.

Unpaid tax and the August land sale

The whole state auctions delinquent land on the same day, the fourth Monday in August (RSMo 140.150). An owner can head it off by paying the Dent County Collector the tax with penalty, interest and costs. For the current list and amounts, call 573-729-3911.

  • Before the list is published, a first class notice goes to the owner of public record.
  • Certified mail is used for a second notice only if assessed valuation is over $1,000.
  • A certified notice returned unsigned is followed by a first class mailing to the owner of record and to the occupant.
  • Not receiving any notice does not cancel the tax.

RSMo 140.405 requires a tax sale buyer to warn owners and lienholders of the right to redeem at least ninety days before taking a deed. Anyone holding an inherited or vacant house should call the Collector early and learn what is owed.

Selling a Dent County house

Here is a sensible order for a Dent County sale. Check the owner name and parcel on the Assessor's GIS map. Ask the Collector for the balance with any penalty and interest. Hand that figure to the title company so the payoff is in the settlement statement. Once the deed records, send the Collector the buyer's name and mailing address. A short list like this keeps the closing date from slipping over a tax question.

Salem is the county seat and Bunker is the other city. The county's 2020 census count was 14,421, down from 15,657 ten years earlier.

Before you list, ask the Collector for the balance on your parcel and make sure the owner name matches your deed. If tax is owed, the title company can pay it from your proceeds at closing, and the Collector only needs the new owner's mailing address afterward. A house inherited from a relative, or one left vacant, is the case where back taxes most often go unnoticed, so check it first.

What is the last day to pay Dent County tax without penalty?

The end of December. Bills go out by November 8 and the penalty begins January 1. Phone 573-729-3911 if yours is missing.

Can Dent County taxes be paid on the web?

Yes, through dentcountycollector.com, where statements can be viewed and paid. The office at 400 N. Main Street in Salem also takes payment on weekdays during business hours.

How is residential property assessed?

At 19% of market value. Farm ground is assessed at 12% of production value and all other property at 32% of true value in money. Full reassessment comes in odd-numbered years, with new construction added every year.

What is the cutoff for an appeal to the local board?

By the second Monday in July under RSMo 137.275. Reach the County Clerk at 573-729-4144 about hearing dates.

When is the personal property list due?

March 1. Property held on January 1 is listed with the Assessor between January 1 and March 1, and a late list can draw a penalty of up to $105.00. Newcomers must set up an account.

Moniteau County in brief

About 15,400 people live in Moniteau, a rural central Missouri county that sits inside the Jefferson City metro area. California is both seat and biggest city. Households number 5,729 and average 2.45 people, and roughly four in five homes are owner-occupied. Residents value a typical house at $181,900 against a median rent of $735. Builders pulled just 6 permits in 2025, which leaves resale houses as most of what a buyer sees. Clarksburg, Jamestown, Lupus and Tipton are the other towns, with Fortuna and Latham as named communities, and six school districts cover the county.

Which Moniteau County offices handle your tax bill?

Visit the courthouse at 200 E. Main Street in California. The assessor and collector both work weekdays from 8:00 to 4:30, holidays excepted.

  • Assessor, Room 105. Call 573-796-4637 or write assessor@moniteaucountymo.gov. Its job is valuing all taxable real and personal property countywide.
  • Collector, Room 101. Call 573-796-4521. The collector prints the statements, forwards collections to schools and other districts monthly, issues merchant licenses and holds the August sale of delinquent land. Staff work through the noon hour.
  • Recorder, Room 102. The circuit clerk also serves as recorder, at 573-796-2071.

Read each statement closely for the address, listed vehicles and legal description. Payment is possible in person, by phone, through the mail or on the collector's website, with cash, personal check, e-check, money order or credit card.

How a house is valued

Houses are reappraised on a two-year cycle. Section 137.115 sets new assessed values on January 1 of each odd-numbered year, and they hold through the following even-numbered year. New construction is handled separately.

Only part of market value is taxed, and the share depends on subclass. Subclass 1 real property is assessed at 19 percent, subclass 2 at 12 percent and subclass 3 at 32 percent. Personal property is assessed at 33 and one third percent, with lower rates for livestock, farm machinery, poultry and a few other items. The assessor can tell you your parcel's class. A manufactured home lived in as a dwelling is taxed at the residential percentage.

An increase of more than fifteen percent on a subclass 1 parcel, new construction aside, requires an on-site physical inspection first. Viewing from the street is not enough. The owner may ask for the interior to be included, with at least thirty days after written notice to ask.

Tax calendar and due dates

The tax year starts January 1, the valuation date, and payment closes December 31. Personal property lists go to the assessor, and late fees begin if a list comes back after March 1. Anyone living in the county on January 1 should list cars, boats and equipment, and a mobile home on someone else's land goes on the list too. Household goods, inventories, clothing and items of personal use are exempt.

If November ends and no bill has shown up, call the collector right away. A missing bill does not cancel the tax, the penalty or the interest. A divorcing couple should also know that the collector cannot split a statement after it is issued.

How to appeal your assessment

Disputes climb a ladder of three rungs: the assessor, then the county equalization board, then the State Tax Commission. File with the board by the second Monday of July. Once its decision letter is mailed, you have thirty days from the letter's date to go further, a timing rule section 138.430 backs with its "whichever date later occurs" wording.

The commission takes a direct filing, with no board stop, in two situations:

  • Nobody notified the current owner of a new or higher value at least thirty days ahead of the board deadline.
  • A buyer closed less than thirty days after the county mailed the tax statement.

An attorney has to handle any appeal for property held by a corporation, LLC, limited partnership, trust or estate.

Filing a dispute leaves the payment date where it is. To dodge interest, get the whole amount to the collector by December 31 with "paid under protest" on the check and a written note giving your reasons and the value you believe is right. Skip both the protest and the appeal and that year's assessment is final, although next year's can still be challenged.

Programs that lower the bill

The Property Tax Credit Claim draws the most questions. The credit goes to certain seniors and 100 percent disabled individuals: as much as $1,100 for owners who occupy their homes, $750 for renters. Your tax or rent paid and your whole household income, taxable or not, set the amount.

A former prisoner of war with a total service-connected disability has a constitutional exemption on the homestead they own and occupy. To claim it, give the assessor proof of residence, a federal letter confirming the disability and either a DD 214 or an archives or VA letter establishing POW status.

Service members away on military orders owe no interest on late payment, though a collection fee may still apply. Confirm current rules with the assessor or collector before you plan around any program.

Selling with taxes owed

Before signing a sale contract, get today's payoff from the collector, penalty and interest included. Under section 140.150, land carrying unpaid tax can go to the sale held on the fourth Monday of August. Until that day the owner may pay off the taxes, penalty, interest and costs at the collector's window. A first notice goes by mail to the recorded owner, and when assessed value is above $1,000 a certified second notice follows.

Your closing office should pay off the balance with the collector so nothing is left on the parcel. In a cash sale the payoff simply comes out of your proceeds, with no lender weighing in on an open balance. Gather these before you list: the latest tax statement, the legal description, and the payoff figure from the collector. If the value on the statement looks off, raise it with the assessor before the July board deadline so the number a buyer sees is one you can stand behind. Our Missouri property tax guide explains how appeals work statewide, and the Missouri homestead page covers exemptions. The collector's website carries the current levy sheet for anyone estimating a bill.

Frequently asked questions

Which office sends property tax statements in Moniteau County?

The collector in Room 101 at the California courthouse prints and mails them each November. The assessor in Room 105 supplies the values behind them.

What day do unpaid Moniteau County taxes turn delinquent?

Anything still owed after December 31. The collector then offers the land at the August sale, and the owner may still pay before the sale.

By when must I contest a value?

The county board's filing deadline is the second Monday of July. After the board's letter, you have thirty days to continue to the State Tax Commission.

What share of my house's worth is taxed?

Subclass 1 real property is assessed at 19 percent of true value, subclass 2 at 12 percent and subclass 3 at 32 percent. Your assessor can name the class for your parcel.

Is there a credit for older homeowners?

Seniors and 100 percent disabled individuals may file Missouri's Property Tax Credit Claim, which pays up to $1,100 to homeowners who occupy their house. Income and the tax actually paid set the amount.

Which Pettis County offices handle property tax?

The assessor does not set tax rates or district budgets. Schools, cities, fire districts and other districts set their own rates, and the collector collects whatever amount is assigned to each owner.

How a Pettis County house is valued

Real estate is revalued in odd-numbered years. A value set as of that January 1 stays on the books through the following even year, and only new construction or demolition changes it in between. The assessor looks at sales of comparable properties, the condition and physical features of the home, and any building or teardown work.

Fixed percentages turn market value into assessed value:

  • Homes and other residential land: 19 percent
  • Farmland: 12 percent
  • Commercial parcels: 32 percent

Each district's levy is then applied to every $100 of assessed value to produce the bill. RSMo 137.115 backs the percentages. It also stops the assessor from raising a residential parcel by more than 15 percent without a physical inspection, unless the jump comes from new construction.

How to appeal your assessment

The assessor describes three stages. The first is a sit-down at the assessor's office to learn how your number was built and what records support it. Many disputes end right there.

  1. Call the assessor soon after the valuation notice arrives and ask for a meeting.
  2. If that fails, the county clerk provides forms and deadlines for the Board of Equalization, which hears the assessor and then you.
  3. Still unhappy? The State Tax Commission accepts appeals until September 30 or thirty days after the board's last action, whichever is later.

Two state rules favor the owner. A value increase must be reported to the record owner, with the statute setting June 15 as the mailing date (RSMo 137.180). At the board, no one presumes the assessor is right, and if a parcel's assessed value rose 15 percent or more, new construction aside, the assessor carries the burden of proof (RSMo 138.060). The commission route appears in RSMo 138.430.

Vehicles and most equipment are assessed at 33 and one third percent of value, farm equipment and livestock at 12 percent, and a vehicle with historic plates at 5 percent.

Someone moving to Pettis County from another state brings registration papers or titles to the assessor's office to open an account. A person who was not a Missouri resident on January 1 is exempt for that first year and can get a statement of no tax due. Senior tax credit

Pettis County has adopted the Senate Bill 190 program, which gives an eligible senior a credit on the real estate tax bill of a primary residence. The county's FAQ lists the main conditions:

  • The home is the primary residence, lived in 183 days or more a year, and assessed as residential.

The credit equals the difference between the tax owed and what the home owed in the base year. It appears on the statement and is not a refund, and it does not reach back before the base year. Sedalia anchors a county of roughly 682 square miles in west central Missouri, with small towns such as Green Ridge, Houstonia, Hughesville, Ionia, La Monte, Smithton and Windsor around it. December 31. Payments not received by then draw late penalties and fees, so allow time for online and phone payments to process.

Residential property is assessed at 19 percent of market value, agricultural at 12 percent and commercial at 32 percent.

Meet with the assessor first, then go to the county Board of Equalization through the county clerk, and last to the State Tax Commission. The commission deadline is the later of September 30 or 30 days after the board's final action.

Card payments carry a fee of at least $1.55 or 2.45 percent, which the county does not keep. E-checks have no fee but need about ten days to clear.

Who owes the tax is decided on January 1. Even a seller who leaves the next day owes the year's bill, and state law has no proration rule.

So the contract has to divide the year between buyer and seller. Typically the title company deducts the seller's portion from the proceeds and pays the county or credits the buyer. Ring the Collector at 660-438-7721 before signing to learn the full balance, earlier years included.

A value error can't be fixed at the Collector's counter. Take it to the Assessor before you pay.

The same applies to a cash sale. With no lender escrow, the closing agent splits the year as the contract directs and pays the county from the proceeds. Ask the buyer early whether they want the bill paid at closing or left for them to pay by December 31.

The Benton County tax sale

Real estate with two years of unpaid tax goes to auction on the fourth Monday of August. Bidding happens outside the Warsaw courthouse, and the county's tax sale site lists the parcels.

Losing the auction doesn't end your claim right away. RSMo 140.405 obliges the winning bidder to send redemption notice by first class and certified mail no fewer than ninety days before a deed can be taken. Transferring or encumbering the land means redeeming it first.

To sell a delinquent parcel, get the full payoff to the Collector and the title company ahead of the auction. Once redeemed, it can close like any other house.

Paying under protest

If you contest the bill, RSMo 139.031 allows full payment before the delinquency date together with a written statement of why and what value you claim. The Collector sends on the undisputed part and keeps the rest apart.

Sue the Collector in circuit court within ninety days of the protest, unless you already have a timely assessment appeal open with the State Tax Commission or a court. Tax paid by mistake can be refunded or credited if you ask within three years.

Personal property has its own date. Report what you owned on January 1 to the Assessor by March 1 to avoid penalties.

Before you list a Benton County home

A few phone calls up front keep a sale from stalling at the closing table.

  1. Call the Collector at 660-438-7721 and ask for the balance on the parcel, including any earlier year. A parcel with two years unpaid can head to the August auction.
  2. Call the Assessor at 660-438-5323 for real estate questions, or 660-438-5473 if a vehicle or other personal property account is involved. Ask whether the record card matches the house as it stands.
  3. If you plan to dispute the value, remember that the Clerk books Board of Equalization hearings at 660-438-7326.
  4. Tell the title company who gets the statement, since bills go to the owner on file. Mail sent to an old address still counts as your debt.

Keep your paid receipts. The Collector gives out duplicates if you lose one, which can save time when a buyer or lender asks for proof of payment on prior years. If the office is closed, you can still use the drop box on the north side of the courthouse for a December payment.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay property tax in Benton County, Missouri?

Send it to the Collector at P.O. Box 428 in Warsaw, pay at the office, or use the courthouse's north-side drop box. For your parcel's current payoff, call 660-438-7721.

When do Benton County property taxes become delinquent?

Once December 31 ends. A check postmarked later comes back unless late fees are included, and the drop box takes payments until midnight that night.

Does Benton County reassess property every year?

No. Full reassessment happens in odd years, and even years only add new construction and remove lost improvements. The next full one is 2027.

When is the Benton County tax sale?

On the fourth Monday of August, at the courthouse in Warsaw, for real estate with two years of delinquent tax.

Is Benton County property tax prorated when I sell?

The law doesn't prorate it, and the January 1 owner stays liable for the year. Your sale contract sets the split, and the title company handles payment at closing.

Cedar County housing snapshot

Cedar County is rural southwest Missouri. Stockton is the seat, El Dorado Springs is the largest town, and none of the population counts as urban, so a house here is usually in a small town or on open land. Stockton Lake takes up a good share of the county's water area. Two school districts serve it, El Dorado Springs R-II and Stockton R-I.

  • Population, July 1, 2025: 14,888, with 6,985 housing units and 74.1% owner-occupied.
  • Middle value of owner-occupied homes (2020 to 2024): $168,100.
  • Median gross rent: $767. Median household income: $48,181.
  • Building permits issued in 2025: 8.

Only 8 permits in a year means very little new construction competes with resale houses, so condition and price carry most of the weight with buyers.

Who runs property tax

Two elected offices split the work. The Assessor values property. The Collector of Revenue mails bills and collects the money. Neither sets the rate. That comes from the school, fire, ambulance and other districts listed on each statement.

  • Collector of Revenue: 113 South Street, PO Box 280, Stockton, MO 65785, in Room 1 on the main floor of the courthouse. Phone 417.276.6700 ext. 224, fax 417.276.4658.
  • Assessor: courthouse line 417-276-6700. Extensions 258 and 259 take personal property questions.
  • Online payments and bill search run through the Collector's page on cedarcountymo.gov.

The Assessor's own site, cedar.missouriassessors.com, has the parcel search, the real estate and personal property FAQs and the newsletters.

Due dates and how to pay

Statements for land, buildings and personal property are mailed in November. Payment is due by December 31, and for mailed checks the postmark decides. A postmark after December 31 has to include penalty and interest, and the delinquent payment chart on your statement shows the add-on. If December 1 comes and no bill has shown up, call the Collector, since a missing bill doesn't erase the obligation.

  • Online payments carry a 2.4 percent card convenience fee, or a $1.95 fee for an e-check.
  • A mailed payment's receipt takes 7 to 10 days. Online receipts can be printed once the payment posts.
  • A prepay plan divides last year's amount into nine equal installments. You must start by September 30, and the November statement then shows what is left.
  • Personal property is valued on January 1, and the whole year's tax is owed even after the owner moves away.

Real estate tax stays attached to the parcel itself, whoever the owner is.

How the Assessor sets home values

Real property is reassessed every odd-numbered year, and in even years the office adds new construction. Values reflect the property's condition on January 1, so a building torn down after that date is still taxed for the full year. Because 2027 is an odd year, plan for a reassessment then.

Field staff look at the outside of buildings and go inside only if the owner asks. RSMo 137.130 gives the Assessor a right to inspect when information is missing. In 2025 the State Tax Commission ordered a 14.99 percent increase on improved residential and commercial property in the county, with new construction excepted, and Change in Value notices went out in June 2025. If your house sold or was refinanced since, expect a number well above older figures.

Personal property sheets are due before March 1, with late penalties from $15 up to $105 depending on assessed value. The Assessor offers e-filing with the account number and ePIN printed on the sheet.

How to dispute an assessment

Begin by phoning the Assessor to walk through the value. If you still disagree, the next stops are the county board that hears valuation appeals and then the State Tax Commission. Ask the Cedar County Clerk or the Assessor for the board's current forms and hearing dates.

StepTiming

Hearing request to the county board (RSMo 137.275)Lodged by the second Monday of July
Appeal to the State Tax Commission (RSMo 138.430)Within the statutory window or a month after the board decides, whichever comes later

One rule helps an owner whose value jumped. RSMo 138.060 says the board starts with no presumption that the Assessor's number is right. When assessed valuation rose at least 15 percent from the last assessment, the burden of proof falls on the Assessor, unless the rise came from new construction or improvements.

Tax relief for seniors and others

Cedar County adopted the Senate Bill 190 senior tax freeze. Senior tax credit applications are taken from March 15 to May 15, 2027. Seniors and people who are 100 percent disabled can also ask the Assessor for a 948 form, a credit based on the real estate taxes paid during the year.

Disabled-veteran exemptions are a separate matter. Rules have been changing at the state level, and the Assessor says it will apply any new exemption as soon as the law allows. Ask the Assessor before assuming an exemption covers your parcel.

Selling with unpaid taxes

The Collector holds a delinquent land tax sale on the fourth Monday of August each year and issues certificates of purchase and redemptions. Land with back taxes can end up in that sale, so clear the balance or tell the title company early.

  • Ask the Collector for the current balance on the parcel, including penalty and interest.
  • Give the title company the Collector's contact details so the payoff shows up on the settlement statement.
  • After the deed is recorded, tell the Collector and the Assessor the buyer's name and mailing address so the next bill reaches the right person.

Since tax liability stays with the land, a buyer inherits an unpaid balance unless it is settled at closing. Paying it from proceeds keeps your closing clean. Bring the parcel number from your latest statement to the title company, along with the Collector's phone number, so the payoff letter can be ordered the same day you sign the listing. A cash buyer can also take on a parcel with back taxes and let the closing agent settle them, which avoids a lender's demand that the account be cleared first.

Frequently asked questions

When are Cedar County property taxes due?

December 31 each year. Statements are mailed in November, and the postmark on a mailed payment decides whether it is on time. After December 31, penalty and interest apply. If no bill has come by December 1, call 417.276.6700 ext. 224 in Stockton.

Which office answers questions about my value?

The Cedar County Assessor, at 417-276-6700. Personal property questions go to ext. 258 or 259. The Assessor's website has the real estate FAQ, the parcel search and the latest newsletter. The Collector is a separate office and cannot change a value on a statement.

How do I pay online?

Use the Pay/Search link on the Collector's page at cedarcountymo.gov. Cards carry a 2.4 percent convenience fee and e-checks a $1.95 fee. Search by last name then first name with no comma, and print the receipt once the payment is applied.

Can I challenge my property value?

Yes. Talk to the Assessor first, then lodge a hearing request with the county board no later than the second Monday of July, as RSMo 137.275 requires. A further appeal to the State Tax Commission is open within the statutory window or a month after the board decides, whichever comes later.

What if the land has delinquent taxes when I sell?

Pay the balance at or before closing, usually through the title company, because the lien follows the land. The Collector holds a delinquent land tax sale on the fourth Monday of August. Get the exact payoff, with penalty and interest, from the Collector in Stockton.

Where the county offices are

Lawrence County is a Class 3 county run by a three-member commission. Most offices are in Mt. Vernon: the historic courthouse at 1 E. Courthouse Square, the Justice Center at 240 N. The Assessor works from the basement of the Historic Lawrence County Courthouse in Mt. Vernon. Mail goes to P.O. Box 188, Mt. Vernon, MO 65712, the phone is (417) 466-2831, and the office is open 8:00 to 4:00 on weekdays.

The Collector of Revenue is on the first floor of the courthouse at #1 Courthouse Square. Each month's collections are banked with the county treasury, which forwards them to schools, libraries, ambulance and fire districts and special road districts.

How and when to pay

November is mailing month, and statements should reach you by the second week. Each is due on receipt and delinquent once December 31 is over. If nothing has come by Thanksgiving, call 417-466-2410.

Disputing a value does not force early payment. The Commission says you may appeal first and pay afterward, or pay the whole bill by December 31 as a protest, adding a written explanation and your own estimate of market value.

  • August: the Collector's delinquent real estate auction.
  • November: statements are mailed and are due on receipt.
  • December 31: the postmark deadline, after which penalty and interest begin.

A house that lists in spring will usually close before the next bill exists, so the buyer inherits a bill the seller never saw. Settle in the contract who pays the current year and how it is divided, and have the title company confirm that no earlier year is open.

What happens at closing when tax is owed

The title company asks the Collector for the amount due, deducts it from your proceeds and sends the payment before it releases the balance to you. Nothing about that requires you to pay out of pocket in advance.

What can cause delay is a number that moves. Penalty and interest keep building on a delinquent bill, so a payoff taken early may be short by closing day. Ask the Collector how long a figure stays good, and have the title company refresh it near the end. If a statement never reached you, call before you list and say so; the Collector can tell you which years are paid and which are not.

Get a written payoff from the Collector, then have the Assessor confirm the acreage, address and owner of record. It is cheaper to fix a wrong parcel description before a buyer's title search catches it.

Selling for cash does not change the tax. The payoff still comes from the proceeds at closing, but with no buyer loan to approve, you can usually have the figure settled soon after the offer is accepted.

Until the second Monday in July for the county board. The State Tax Commission then allows 30 days from the board's letter.

Who do I call in Galena about my tax bill?

Two county offices share the work. The Assessor builds the list of taxable property, and the Collector of Revenue bills and gathers the money. Both are in Galena.

The Assessor's office also keeps the tax maps, adjusting property lines whenever the Recorder of Deeds forwards a warranty deed, per the Assessor's description of its mapping duties. On the Collector's side, the staff directory names separate deputies for real estate, personal property, merchant licensing and the SB190 tax freeze, so ask for the real estate desk when you call about a house, and keep the parcel number handy.

What is the due date for the 2026 bill?

The Collector's announcement says statements for 2026 went into the mail on Friday, November 13, and online payment has been open since November 6. Payment is due by December 31, and a bill still open on January 1 is delinquent.

Anything sent by post must carry a U.S. Post Office postmark dated December 31 or earlier. The Collector's home page adds several practical notes:

  • Card numbers are no longer taken verbally over the phone. Pay at the office or call the number printed on your statement.
  • Debit and credit card payments carry a fee of 2.4%, with a $1.95 floor.
  • A drop box at the north entrance of the Historic Courthouse is emptied daily.
  • A paid receipt can be printed, or shown on a phone, at the license bureau.

Read your statement for errors, including the mailing address. To change an address, call 417-357-6124.

Is the senior tax freeze open right now?

No. The Collector's home page says the application process for the Senior Citizen Property Tax Credit Freeze is closed. The staff list includes a lead for the SB190 tax freeze, who is the person to ask about the next window.

A second benefit comes from the state: the Missouri Property Tax Credit Claim, filed with the Department of Revenue, refunds part of the tax or rent paid for some seniors, disabled owners and renters. Phone the Collector's office at 417-357-6124 to find out whether you fit either program before the next filing season.

How do I argue against my assessed value?

Phone the Assessor on (417) 357-6145 and ask this year's Board of Equalization deadline. RSMo 138.060 tells the county board to decide valuation appeals in a summary way and adds that no presumption favors the assessor. Where a parcel's assessed value jumped by 15% or more over the previous assessment, other than through new construction or improvement, the assessor must show the figure is not above market value.

If you still owe the bill while arguing, RSMo 139.031 permits payment under protest. The full bill is paid before delinquency, a written statement of your reasons goes to the collector, and a circuit court action starts within 90 days. Penalties and interest start running. RSMo 140.150 allows delinquent land to go to sale each August, on the fourth Monday. The collector writes to the owner of record before publication, and the owner may clear the tax, penalty, interest and costs any time ahead of the sale.

Is Stone County growing, and what do homes cost?

Population is rising. The Census Bureau's April 2020 base was 31,079 and the July 2025 estimate is 32,503, a gain of 4.6%. Over the same stretch St. Louis County and Stoddard County each lost 1.4%. Stone County belonged to the Branson micropolitan area until 2023, and the Branson West Municipal Airport sits two nautical miles west of the city of Branson West.

The Census lists 21,225 housing units for July 2025 and 13,530 households for 2020 to 2024, so the housing stock sits well above the count of households. It lies in southwest Missouri along the Arkansas line, bordered by Christian, Taney, Barry and Lawrence counties and by Carroll County, Arkansas. Branson West, Reeds Spring, Crane, Hurley and Blue Eye round out the list of cities and villages, and part of the Mark Twain National Forest lies inside the county. Water covers 47 of its 511 square miles, or 9.2%.

The county counted 9,921 residents in 1970 and 31,076 in 2020. It was organized on February 10, 1851, and takes its name from William Stone, an early Maryland settler. The Census table adds the housing details.

Libraries operate in Blue Eye, Crane, Galena and Kimberling City. Employment reached 5,681 in 2023, up 8.2% on 2022, and retail sales totaled $359,943,000 in 2022.

Frequently asked questions

Where can I find the Stone County Collector?

The Bollinger County housing market

Everything in Bollinger County is rural: 10,567 people in 2020, spread over 618 square miles of land. It sits within the Cape Girardeau metro area, and commutes average 35.5 minutes. Expect a small, local buyer pool of long-time owners, family transfers and people willing to drive.

With so little new construction, existing houses carry the market. For those buyers, a clean tax record and a prompt, well-documented closing are what keep a contract together.

When Bollinger County taxes are due

December 31 is the last day in every Missouri county, Bollinger included. After it, unpaid balances start picking up interest and penalties, and RSMo 139.100 counts a mailed payment as timely when its postmark falls inside the period. For bill timing, accepted payment types and the current mailing address, call 573-238-1900 and ask for the Collector.

Land that stays unpaid is hit by RSMo 140.100, which adds an 18 percent penalty on that year's delinquency, or no more than 2 percent a month if the owner redeems ahead of a sale. Sales are held on the fourth Monday in August.

How the Bollinger County tax sale works

RSMo 140.150 puts land with unpaid taxes or special assessments up for sale on the fourth Monday of each August. Owners get several safeguards first.
